entries.title: Senate Advances Russia Sanctions Bill
entries.summary: The legislation cleared a procedural hurdle hours after the funeral of Lindsey Graham, who championed the package.
entries.content:
The Senate on Tuesday advanced sweeping new sanctions targeting Russia, moving long-stalled legislation that supporters say would squeeze one of the Kremlin’s most important sources of wartime revenue.

The Senate voted 86-12, clearing the way for legislation named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican whose death this month spurred supporters to try to get it done.

The legislation would authorize the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the largest purchasers of Russian energy, while also targeting Russian officials, oligarchs, banks and other supporters of Moscow’s war effort and vessels in Russia’s so-called shadow fleet.

The legislation split Democrats, with 11 voting “no” amid concerns about the bill expanding President Donald Trump’s authority to impose tariffs on foreign countries.

Negotiators in recent weeks had narrowed the measure from an earlier proposal that called for tariffs as high as 500% to broaden support. The administration would retain discretion over the precise tariff rate and could waive individual sanctions or tariffs after certifying to Congress that doing so was in the national interest.

Supporters hailed the procedural vote, taken after Graham’s funeral and a Washington visit from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as a long-awaited bipartisan rebuke of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“With this vote, we are going to show Putin he can't bully Ukraine,” said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. “America stands behind Ukraine. We are going to back Ukraine, and they're going to win and beat Putin.”

After Zelenskyy met with Trump at the White House to discuss Patriot missile coproduction and diplomatic efforts, he met privately with senators in the evening as the chamber prepared to vote. He then watched the vote from the Senate gallery.

“We are thankful that this bill is very important,” Zelenskyy said after meeting with senators. “Sanctions pressure on Russia is very important. It's not only about how to stop financing this war. But it's also a big signal to Europe, a big signal to Ukraine, big support of our people. So I'm very thankful.”

The visit also underscored Graham’s role as one of Ukraine’s staunchest advocates in Congress. Zelenskyy said he opened his Oval Office meeting by offering condolences over Graham’s death, calling him “a true friend of Ukraine.”

Zelenskyy returned to Washington for Graham’s funeral less than three weeks after Graham traveled to Kyiv to discuss the sanctions package with him. Days later, Graham announced the bill had Trump’s support after months of delay.

If the Senate ultimately passes the legislation before its August recess, it would hand Trump one of the most aggressive sanctions tools Congress has considered since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, while cementing one of Graham’s final legislative achievements.

“There are a number of stars aligned,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the bill’s lead Democratic sponsor, told NOTUS. “Ukraine's turning the tide, Trump's support, Zelensky visiting, and very definitely Lindsey Graham's passionate advocacy for it — and obviously for me they're all important, and they've enabled us to come closer to the finish line than ever before.”

But several Democrats expressed concerns ahead of the vote about Trump’s tariff authority.

“The sanctions on [Russia’s] energy sector is something, definitely, I support,” said Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia), who voted “no.” “But this bill in its current form gives the president a wide margin in the continuing advancement of this tariff regime, and I don't know that we have much evidence that he's going to use it to do what we need him to do.”

The version of the bill that advanced Tuesday included several new provisions. It would extend existing sanctions authority over Iran's energy and weapons sectors through 2031. Trump insisted that Iran be included in the legislation, but Blumenthal credited his new co-sponsor, Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina), with the provision. 

The Iran provision also has relevance for Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian president has repeatedly urged allies to treat Moscow and Tehran as linked military partners, citing Iran’s supply of attack drones that Russia has used against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.

The bill also includes a five-year sunset for the new Russia sanctions authorities.

The additions appeared intended to help address concerns from some Democrats that the bill’s tariff authorities were too sweeping, though supporters argued those fears were overstated.

The bill would also limit when the administration could lift the Russia sanctions. The president generally could not terminate them unless Moscow signed a peace agreement accepted by Ukraine’s government and ended its military campaign and efforts to subvert Kyiv.

If the president determines those conditions have been met and moves to lift the sanctions, it would trigger a congressional review period during which lawmakers could attempt to block it through a joint resolution of disapproval.

“This is not a new idea,” said Senate Foreign Relations Chair Jim Risch (R-Idaho). “The president has finally signaled that he's ready to go. We did negotiate some additional provisions.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said ahead of the vote that he hoped a strong showing would put pressure on holdouts in each party to agree to fast-track a vote to pass the bill before the recess.

Tuesday’s vote would not guarantee final passage. Without a time agreement, the Senate would still have to complete additional procedural steps and resolve any demands for amendment votes.

The legislation would also have to pass the House, where lawmakers have already raised separate concerns over the tariff authority it would offer to Trump.

entries.title: Federal Immigration Agents Called Latinos Racial Slurs While Conducting Stops, Video Shows
entries.summary: Body camera footage and texts showed federal immigration agents using racist and crude language when discussing immigrants, according to court filings submitted Monday.
entries.content:
As federal immigration agents swarmed Los Angeles last summer under orders from the Trump administration, some used crude language and racial slurs as they moved to detain immigrants.

“Yeah, just plug us in wherever you see some tonks,” said one officer, using a derogatory term for the sound a flashlight makes when it hits someone’s head. “We’ll jump out.”

The remarks were recorded in body camera footage that was among the multitude of videos, texts and other transcripts submitted Monday by the American Civil Liberties Union in federal court after a monthslong, court-ordered discovery. Monday’s motion — filed by the ACLU, Public Counsel and other advocacy organizations — requested a preliminary injunction to stop federal immigration agents from using an individual’s “apparent status as low-income or working-class and Latino” to conduct detentive stops.

“This filing should shock the conscience,” Mayra Joachin, deputy director of immigrants’ rights at the ACLU of Southern California, said in a statement. “Evidence gathered from the government has confirmed what our communities have known all along: immigration officers are flagrantly violating the law by detaining people without justification and often primarily because of the color of their skin.”

ACLU Body Cam Footage.mp4
Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Border Patrol and other federal agents carried out sweeping raids in Los Angeles last year as part of the White House’s aggressive mass-deportation push. The federal immigration agents would often target sites where day laborers would congregate and indiscriminately carry out arrests.

The activities sparked tense protests, leading to President Donald Trump unlawfully deploying the National Guard.

“Our agents are focused on protecting the American people — not entertaining performative outrage,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement Tuesday to NOTUS when asked for comment.

The videos, which did not clearly distinguish from which federal agencies the agents came, included body camera footage from June 2025 to September 2025. Agents were not identified in the videos or court filings. The Los Angeles Times and CalMatters were first to report the court filings.

In one video recorded Aug. 6, Border Patrol agents are seen in the back of a cargo van. One agent points to a backpack and asks, “Who’s backpack is that? Tonk’s backpack?”

Another video recorded on June 12 showed an agent lament, “One tonk fucking got away, dude.” The agent repeats the phrase again later before touching the body camera, asking, “How do you turn off the camera?”

Footage from June 19 showed two federal agents discussing an operation they just completed.

“There was a guy, I'm pretty sure he's wet,” one agent said, using a racial slur for immigrants. “He was just sitting in that minivan."

Federal agents were also recorded mocking a vulgar chant from anti-ICE protesters. Another video recorded on Sept. 23 contains a conversation between two officers that appears to be about a woman that was tracking their whereabouts.

“She's a white lady, too,” one officer is heard saying in the footage.

“They like being oppressed for other races,” his colleague replies. “I don't know why.”

In a series of text messages exchanged on July 2 one federal agent asks if they could “pull facial rec off of profile pies of people who are self admitting in tik tok comments to being illegal.”

The agent sent a photo which was redacted in the court document, adding, “This bitch good enough to facial rec?”

A colleague replied that the photo did not result in any matches.

“Some of these people are stupid,” the first agent replied. “Why would you post on social media that you're wet.”

In a separate text exchange on July 4, an agent wrote, “tonks everywhere selling food for the 4th festivities in long beach right now.”

Armando Gudino, executive director of the Los Angeles Worker Center Network, a plaintiff in the lawsuit along with five Latino workers and other organizations, said the exhibits “reinforce the urgent need for accountability and an immediate end to these unconstitutional and illegal practices against our communities.”

A federal district court issued a temporary restraining order on July 11, 2025, that barred indiscriminate immigration stops. The Supreme Court put that ruling on hold in August 2025, allowing the federal government to continue the practice while litigation continued.

A hearing for Monday’s motion is scheduled for Sept. 24.

entries.title: Megadonor Received Trump Pardon Three Days After Donation to Pennsylvania Congressman
entries.summary: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie’s campaign says the lawmaker, who met with Trump days before, played no role in the pardon.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump recently pardoned a major Republican donor three days after the man — a key figure in the Jack Abramoff fraud and lobbying scandal — made a political donation to Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pennsylvania), who’s facing one of the nation’s most contested House races.

The megadonor, Adam Kidan, donated $2,600 to Mackenzie's leadership PAC on June 30, according to Federal Election Commission records. Trump traveled to Mackenzie’s eastern Pennsylvania district on June 23 to campaign with him. The president pardoned Kidan on July 3.

Mackenzie’s office told NOTUS that the Republican congressman did not speak with the White House or Trump about the pardon, but it declined to answer questions about whether the congressman intends to keep Kidan’s donation.

“Congressman Mackenzie has never advocated for a pardon from the President on anyone’s behalf,” Mackenzie spokesperson Arnaud Armstrong said in a statement.

The White House and Kidan did not respond to NOTUS’ requests for comment.

Mackenzie faces Democratic challenger Bob Brooks to represent Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District in what the Cook Political Report ranks as a “toss-up” race.

In an email to NOTUS, Brooks campaign manager Jenna Kaufman said: “Three days after a convicted fraudster cut Ryan Mackenzie a massive campaign check, that same fraudster walked away with a presidential pardon. That is corruption in plain sight.”

Kidan, who served about two-and-a-half years in prison in 2006 after pleading guilty to conspiracy and wire fraud, has donated millions to Republican causes over the years. He gave around $270,000 to Trump-affiliated committees during the 2024 election cycle, according to federal records, and has hosted fundraisers at Mar-a-Lago.
AdamKidan (1860x2816, AR: 0.66)He has also contributed to a number of Republican campaigns throughout the 2026 midterms, including donations in 2025 to three swing-district House members from Pennsylvania: Rob Bresnahan, Brian Fitzpatrick and Scott Perry. He has also supported Pennsylvania Treasurer Stacy Garrity’s bid for governor in the state.

In April, Kidan donated $7,231 to former Rep. Mike Rogers’ Senate bid in Michigan, $3,500 to Rep. Zach Nunn’s reelection in Iowa and $22,445 to Rep. Jim Jordan’s joint fundraising committee in Ohio, federal records show.

Kidan’s donation to Mackenzie’s leadership PAC is his most recent federal political contribution on record, FEC records indicate.

As part of his sentencing, Kidan and Abramoff were ordered to pay a total of $217 million in restitution. It’s unclear whether Kidan paid the full amount, and Trump’s pardon is likely to erase any remaining financial obligations.

entries.title: Debbie Wasserman Schultz’s Run Is Infuriating Black Democrats. She Might Win Anyway.
entries.summary: If Wasserman Schultz wins the race to represent a historically Black district, it would be “the greatest civil rights threat that’s facing us today,” one Democratic candidate said.
entries.content:
When candidates running for Florida’s 20th Congressional District gathered for a forum hosted by the local chapter of the NAACP in late July, Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, the only white candidate in the race, wasn’t there.

“If someone didn’t come, it wasn’t because they weren’t asked, it’s because they chose not to come and ask for your vote,” Marsha Ellison, president of the NAACP Broward County chapter told the audience, which was mostly made up of people of color.

The candidates never directly named Wasserman Schultz — but her decision to run in the district, which has historically been represented by Black lawmakers and has a plurality Black population, has drawn the ire of her opponents and overshadowed much of the race. Wasserman Schultz lives in Florida’s recently drawn 22nd District, which leans Republican. The 20th District is now the safest blue seat in the state.

The anger at Wasserman Schultz is palpable and doesn’t seem to be going away anytime soon, but it may not matter: Polling in the race has been limited, but Wasserman Schultz is seen as the lead candidate in the race due to the rest of the field splitting the vote. The four Black Democratic candidates in the race initially planned to consolidate behind one person to defeat Wasserman Schultz. However, they were unable to decide who should run and who should drop out.

While the NAACP forum was largely focused on the candidates’ legislative ideas, many candidates criticized Wasserman Schultz’s decision to run.

Luther “Uncle Luke” Campbell, a rapper and Democratic congressional candidate, said that allowing Wasserman Schultz to represent the historically Black district would be “the greatest civil rights threat that’s facing us today.”

“If we allow her to win, we will not win the general,” Campbell said. “The world is watching congressional district 20, and don’t you miss this opportunity.”

The NAACP forum was convened after the Broward County Democratic Black Caucus condemned Wasserman Schultz for suggesting that the group was endorsing her in the race. Wasserman Schultz’s campaign website listed the caucus in its endorsements page, then quietly deleted it after the caucus complained. The group accused Wasserman Schultz of “dishonest intentions” at the time, but Corey Shearer, the caucus’ president, told NOTUS that Wasserman Schultz apologized for the incident and explained that the endorsements listed were from 2022.

However, he said, that doesn’t change his anger that she’s running in a district that has long been represented by a Black representative.

“This is a historical seat for many of us,” Shearer said. “There’s no way, no how, that we want to give that legacy up. And so that’s what Debbie Wasserman Schultz is forcing upon us.”

“The Black community should be able to celebrate that, and our celebration is just ripped away by this move from Debbie Wasserman Schultz, somebody who we looked at as an ally, but it just seems like she was more familiar, and she’s using that familiarity to take an easy way out and look to take our seat,” Shearer said.

The caucus held a debate for candidates in the race last Monday, but Wasserman Schultz also did not attend.

Wasserman Schultz’s campaign did not respond to a list of questions from NOTUS. In a statement, a spokesperson said the “Congresswoman was representing her constituents in DC for votes during both the events in question. Both organizations were informed of this conflict that prevented her from attending.”

Some of the candidates challenging Wasserman Schultz also denounced the Congressional Black Caucus for not publicly speaking out against Wasserman Schultz.

“Our House is not in order because the Congressional Black Caucus … is not on our side,” Campbell said at the NAACP forum. “They allowed a white woman to come in this district knowing that [Republicans] are trying to … gerrymand the vote and take Black representation that has been here for 30 years.”

Former Broward County Mayor Dale Holness, a Democrat, concurred.

“It’s very discouraging, disappointing that the Congressional Black Caucus has not sought to make statements and to stand and say, ‘Look this is wrong,’” Holness said.

The CBC and its campaign arm declined to comment for this story. CBC Chair Yvette Clarke has said she did not encourage Wasserman Schultz to run in the district, despite Wasserman Schultz’s suggestions to the contrary. The CBC PAC does not generally get involved in primaries with multiple Black candidates, though members have endorsed in races in an individual capacity.

Three members of the caucus previously told NOTUS they do not expect the CBC PAC to back the congresswoman in the race. One member at the time called Wasserman Schultz a “friend” to the caucus, so the CBC would likely remain “neutral.”

But House Democrats aren’t running to defend Wasserman Schultz either.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, for example, has declined to endorse Wasserman Schultz in the race.

“I’m looking forward to getting involved in the August primaries, of which there’ll be primaries on Aug. 4th; there will be primaries on Aug. 11th; and then the Florida primaries will be in Aug. 18th,” Jeffries said last Thursday when asked if he’d be endorsing Wasserman Schultz in the race. He called her a “highly effective member of the U.S. Congress and a valuable member of both the leadership team and the House Democratic Caucus.”

Outgoing Rep. Frederica Wilson, who refers to herself as the highest-ranking Black elected official in Florida and represents a neighboring district, recently wrote an op-ed calling the 20th District “a seat paid for by generations of Black sacrifice.” Wilson’s piece does not name Wasserman Schultz.

“If Black lives matter, then the history of Black representation matters too,” Wilson wrote. “We deserve a seat at every table where decisions about our lives, our children, our communities and our future are made. That seat was not given to us. It was earned through generations of Black sacrifice.”

“It is the seat that Black history built,” Wilson continued. “Now it is our responsibility to make sure history never has to build it again.”

Wilson told NOTUS in mid-July that the op-ed was not meant to urge voters to not support Wasserman Schultz but to give context to voters.

“I just wanted the district to know the historical nature of that district.” She added that she had not spoken to Wasserman Schultz since she first announced her candidacy.

“She feels like she should be able to run where she wants to,” Wilson said. But she added, “It took us 117 years to get that district, so I wanted them to be sure when they voted that they were willing to make that sacrifice and go back.”

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) has weighed in on the race and formally endorsed activist Elijah Manley over Wasserman Schultz. Khanna called Manley “bold and progressive” and told NOTUS that his staff had reached out to Wasserman Schultz’s team before the endorsement was announced.

“At a time where Black political rights are under attack, I find it wrong for a heavily Black majority district not to be represented by an African American who connects in that community,” Khanna said.

While some candidates acknowledged it would easier to beat her if she was running against just one person, they’re hoping the backlash over this race will be enough for her to lose the primary.

“If she gets back to Congress, if she somehow wins this race, she will be persona non grata,” Manley told NOTUS in June. “Nobody is going to want to touch her because she will have proceeded in doing what the Republicans want: taking away not just Black representation, but pushing her own career at the expense of the public because this is all about Debbie.”

entries.title: Inside the Push to Claw Back Graham Platner’s Campaign Money
entries.summary: “Anything that we can do to try to take resources out of the hands of predators is worth it,” Cheyenne Hunt told NOTUS.
entries.content:
Cheyenne Hunt watched Rep. Eric Swalwell use campaign funds for legal fees after sexual assault allegations chased him out of Congress. She decided to do something to not watch Graham Platner do the same.

Hunt, a prominent activist and lawyer, launched her organization Reckoning Action in response to the accusations against Swalwell with the goal of ending misogyny in the workplace. After Swalwell, she knew she “had to get a little bit scrappier about how we do this,” Hunt told NOTUS in an interview.

Ultimately, her organization decided to text Platner’s donors directly and teach them how they can get refunds from his campaign.

“Anything that we can do to try to take resources out of the hands of predators is worth it,” Hunt said.

Swalwell dropped out of the California governor’s race and resigned from Congress in early April after multiple women, including one of his former staffers, accused him of sexual assault. He has denied the accusations. Recent Federal Election Commission filings show that Swalwell spent $50,000 in campaign money on defense attorney Sara Azari, who specializes in “#metoo defense,” according to her website. Days after Swalwell resigned, Azari’s firm hired a private investigator who looked into the sexual assault allegations, NOTUS first reported.

Platner, who ended his Senate campaign after being accused of sexual assault, presented a different challenge for Reckoning Action. The group sought legal advice and then informed the women who accused Platner of sexual assault “that there was a good chance that they were being watched and looked into,” Hunt said.

“That is deeply unsettling for survivors after having to go through this incredibly invasive process of bringing that forward,” Hunt said. Platner had $1.7 million cash on hand at the end of last month, according to the most recent FEC data available, and Hunt was concerned that he could use that money “against these survivors.”

Platner’s campaign did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment.

Reckoning Action sent automated texts signed by Hunt to donors with the following message: “If you donated to Graham Platner and feel betrayed, you’re not alone. You signed up to help elect a champion for freedom and equality and take back the Senate — not to fund a predator.” The text linked to a Reckoning Action website with instructions on how to get the refunds.

Hunt told NOTUS that in the hours after they sent that text to “thousands” of donors on July 16, more than 300 people visited the landing page.

Many political donors use the platform ActBlue to contribute to Democratic campaigns. The site allows refunds within 90 days of the payment. Reckoning Action advised donors to contact ActBlue if the donation is older than 90 days or to contact Platner’s campaign directly to request a refund.

The FEC does not allow campaign funds to be used for personal use, but it does allow that money to be used to cover legal expenses related to campaign activity, “where such expenses would not have occurred had the individual not been a candidate or officeholder,” according to its official website.

There’s nothing that directly prohibits a candidate or an elected official from using campaign funds to fight sexual misconduct allegations.

While Hunt and her organization reached out to Platner’s financial supporters, they were also in touch with lawmakers about changing the law. On Tuesday, Reps. Ro Khanna (D-California) and Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida) introduced the No Campaign Funded Cover-Ups Act, a bill that would prohibit candidates and elected officials on the federal level from using campaign money to cover costs related to sexual misconduct claims.

It’s unclear whether the bill will become law, even with bipartisan support.

“Survivors must be heard and respected. Our bipartisan legislation addresses a basic principle: money donated to support a political campaign should not become a personal legal-defense fund for alleged sexual misconduct,” Khanna said in a statement.

Luna concurred in a statement: “If a candidate is accused of sexual assault, sexual abuse, or sexual harassment, campaign donations and legal expense funds should never become a personal bailout. If you commit sexual misconduct, you should foot the bill, not the donors who put their trust in you.”

Platner has denied he sexually assaulted anyone. In an 11-minute video posted on X, he said the allegations were “false” and were “used by the political establishment” to kick him off the ballot in the Maine Senate race.

The reactions from donors to Reckoning Action’s text were mixed.

“Those that were negative definitely echoed the sentiments in his video,” Hunt said. “This concept of not really taking accountability, and that this was something that was happening to him versus a product of his own misconduct and his own lack of honesty. So that was hard.”

“That’s just so disconnected from reality,” Hunt added.

But Platner’s many scandals have already made a dent in his campaign finances. His campaign committee refunded more than $43,000 to donors from late May to June 30, according to its most recent financial report. Those refunds happened at a time when he was dealing with reports of sexual text messages with women outside of his marriage.

“I’m feeling pretty optimistic that we will have put another sizable dent in that campaign account,” Hunt said.

The discussion around sexual misconduct in Congress has spurred lawmakers to create legislation to address sexual misconduct, beyond the Khanna-Luna bill. Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colorado) recently introduced a resolution to prohibit House lawmakers from having romantic relationships with any House employee.

The Republican and Democratic women’s caucuses are preparing to release recommendations after the August recess around overhauling how the House handles sexual misconduct allegations. Both Speaker Mike Johnson and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries have blessed the effort.

“We’re protecting women. We’re protecting the staff,” Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, told reporters last week. “We’re protecting the really brilliant people who choose to come and work for us.”

entries.title: As Training Camp Begins, Commanders Say They Are ‘Happy’ With Receivers
entries.summary: Despite months of speculation about Brandon Aiyuk and others, GM Adam Peters said the team is satisfied with its weapons.
entries.content:
Despite months of online chatter and media speculation, the Commanders believe they are set at the wide receiver position as the team begins training camp Wednesday.

At a Tuesday evening press conference with head coach Dan Quinn, general manager Adam Peters said he feels comfortable with the 11 receivers Washington has on the roster, emphasizing classroom learning, the competitiveness within the group and the leadership of Pro Bowl veteran Terry McLaurin.

“[We’re] really happy with who's in that room, really happy with how the guys progressed in the offseason and stepped up,” Peters said. “I think they're going to take another step in this training camp.”

Despite the confidence, the GM added that those beliefs could change over the course of camp. Of the receivers on the roster, only McLaurin had more than 350 receiving yards last season.

“If we have ways to get better, we're always going to look into that and assess the decision if it's the right move for our team or not,” Peters said. “And if we do think it is, we're not afraid to do that.”

San Francisco 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk has been at the center of most offseason chatter, as the former All-Pro has publicly angled to join his college quarterback, Jayden Daniels, in Washington. Even as Aiyuk has increasingly posted to social media about the possibility of a move, Washington has declined to publicly discuss the 28-year-old.

San Francisco has yet to officially release Aiyuk, although it is widely believed he will not play another snap for the 49ers.

At Tuesday’s press conference, Peters was asked if a prospective player's social media activity is taken into account when considering an acquisition. The question got a laugh out of Peters and Quinn.

“We do look at everything, and we want to make sure it's the right player to be in our locker room, in our bloodstream, in our culture,” Peters said.

While Washington hasn’t made a splashy acquisition at receiver, Peters believes the team has taken the requisite steps to make Daniels’ job easier. The general manager noted the signing of tight end Chig Okonkwo, the offseason overhaul of the team’s defense and the scheming by new offensive coordinator David Blough.

“There's a great energy in the building on both sides, so I think when you bring all those things together … the staff has done a really good job of surrounding him with opportunity to win,” Peters said.

On the other side of the football, cornerback Trey Amos should be practicing “soon” after missing all of spring practice rehabbing the fractured fibula he sustained in Week 10 last year. Peters said Amos dealt with soft tissue soreness earlier in the offseason and the team is taking a cautionary approach to his return.

To shore up the defensive backfield, Washington signed veteran Rasul Douglas on July 9. The 10-year veteran started 13 games for the Dolphins last season, totaling 13 pass deflections and a 54% completion percentage allowed in coverage.

“He's played at a high level,” Peters said. “He started a lot of games recently, and he always performs.”

Neither Quinn nor Peters provided further detail on the team’s decision to fire tight ends coach Ben Steele on Monday. Steele, who was hired in February, was arrested on June 7 and charged with driving while intoxicated.

“A lot of thought was put into that decision, and it's just unfortunate,” Quinn said.

Offensive assistant Wes Welker, a former All-Pro wide receiver, will fill the role, though no official title change has happened yet. Welker coached the unit during spring practices after Steele’s arrest.

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (July 31)
entries.summary: Canadian invasion at the Anthem, Latin jazz at Glen Echo Park, and “Sleeping Beauty” in the woods at Wolf Trap.
entries.content:
Thursday

Passport to Patriotism at the Art Museum of the Americas
201 18th Street NW, D.C., 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., free (through Oct. 18)

If the wife of a Trump golf club manager curated a contemporary museum exhibition, what art would she hang on the walls? This is not a theoretical question. The Organization of American States tapped Erin Scavino, the wife of Dan Scavino, Trump’s longtime aide now serving as the White House director of the Presidential Personnel Office, to helm Passport to Patriotism. The exhibit, celebrating America’s 250th birthday, opens Thursday and runs through Oct. 18. Erin Scavino has no background in art curation or art history, but she does run the State Department’s Art in Embassies program and chose a mix of American flag photography and mixed-media pop-art paintings for her first big curation project.

“The President’s Own” Latin Jazz Ensemble at Glen Echo Park
7300 MacArthur Blvd., Glen Echo, Md., 7:30 p.m., free 

Lose the lottery for Jazz in the Garden again? Sorry. But if you have a car, try jazz at Glen Echo instead. Tonight "The President's Own" Latin Jazz Ensemble, featuring musicians from D.C.’s top U.S. Marine Corps band, makes its annual appearance at the historic Glen Echo Park. The setlist includes tunes by Chick Corea, Tito Puente’s “Cha Cha Cha,” and for the Disney demographic, Alan Menken’s “Under the Sea” calypso.

More to explore: Faction of Fools’ “Leftover Lazzi: A Commedia Cabaret” at Capitol Hill Arts Workshop

Friday

The Funset at Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company
641 D Street NW, D.C., 6 p.m., free

The Penn Quarter theater and Downtown DC BID team up to offer this free indoor dance party with tunes spun by DJ Jahsonic and Harry Hotter. Guzzle gratis Topo Chico while supplies last, and watch local artist Urshula Dunn create a live installation in the theater lobby.

Otakon at the Washington Convention Center
8 a.m. to 10 p.m., $70 adults, children 8 and under free

Cosplay the day away at this 30th annual gathering for fans of all things Asian sci-fi, including anime, music and video games. Festivities include a live-art action (Ballroom C), 30 custom-painted cars (Hall D) plus a K-Pop concert, dance parties and Lyra’s Formal Ball. Dress code: Whatever the character you’re portraying would wear to prom.

More to explore: A live taping of the Broadway musical “Hadestown” screens at local cinemas

Saturday

All the Feelings Tour with Metric, Broken Social Scene and Stars
At the Anthem, 901 Wharf St. NW, D.C., 7 p.m., $74

Tariffs, bans on American booze and the 51st State blues. Canadians have lots of feelings about Washington at the moment. For more positive vibes, head to the Anthem to catch Canadian supergroup Broken Social Scene, plus Metric and Stars, on the All the Feelings tour. The three bands have long shared personnel but rarely share a tour bus. This is your chance to see Stars and Metric form a brass section for their pals, as well as play their own up-tempo, angst-fueled sets.

Washington Sculptors Group: Sculpture NOW 2026 at Harmony Hall Arts Center
10701 Livingston Rd., Fort Washington, Md., opening reception 2 to 4 p.m., free.

Men on horseback may be the most common monuments in the District, but more than 400 local artists belong to this society promoting three-dimensional artwork. The Washington Sculptors Group kicks off its annual juried group show this weekend and keeps the doors open through Sept. 5.

More to explore: 
Celebrate Dark Star Park Day in Rosslyn

Sunday

Maryland Youth Ballet performs “Sleeping Beauty” at Wolf Trap

entries.title: 'Systemic Breakdown'
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: a D.C. police probe, an unsigned budget and the return of Max Scherzer.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

THE LATEST

D.C.’s police department is facing more scrutiny about its crime data. 

According to an investigation by the D.C. inspector general’s office that was released Tuesday, the department has experienced a “prolonged, systemic breakdown” in its crime reporting and lacks adequate controls to ensure its data is reliable.

NOTUS’ Jenny Gathright reports that the investigation adds to a growing list of probes examining crime classification at the police department, an issue that has put city law enforcement in the public spotlight and the Trump administration’s crosshairs.

While past investigations accused department brass of pressuring subordinates to underreport crime, the inspector general’s report tackles more systemic problems in the department that could lead to inaccurate data.

Classifying and reporting crime is one of the central responsibilities of any police department. Crime data informs staffing decisions, helps residents understand what is happening in their neighborhoods and aids the public in holding the government accountable. While the IG’s investigation did not examine whether the city’s crime statistics are accurate, it did find that the department lacks a system for ensuring reporting errors are routinely corrected.

One example: An independent unit responsible for reviewing police reports and crime classifications was shut down in 2013, and the department only recently launched an effort to revive it.

Interim Police Chief Jeffery Carroll took a cooperative tone in response to the findings, agreeing to all of the report’s major recommendations and vowing “strict accountability” going forward.



DEEP DIVE

Muriel Bowser is backing away from the city’s 2027 budget. In what’s mostly a symbolic move, the mayor said Tuesday that she won’t be signing the budget bill for the coming year.

In a letter to D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson, Bowser said she was displeased with some of the spending decisions made by lawmakers, accusing them of choosing to “kick the can down the road” on fiscal challenges to come. She specifically warned of an $837 million “fiscal cliff” the city could face next year, when it’s likely to have a new democratic socialist mayor and more progressive council.

Bowser’s decision caps years of growing tension between her and the council over spending. The conflict goes both ways: Lawmakers say that for all the talk of fiscal rectitude, Bowser herself has been more than willing to engage in the same budget gimmicks she’s now criticizing.

Still, lawmakers say they are aware that next year’s budget deliberations will probably be even harder than they were this year. This fall, the council is expected to consider a variety of revenue-raising proposals to address a growing gap between what the city spends and what it takes in. At the same time, Republicans in the House are threatening to prohibit D.C. from considering any tax increases at all.





FROM THE DISTRICT

A key witness testified that the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool’s lining was already seriously damaged by the time former Olympian David Hearn touched it, NOTUS’ Raymond Fernández reports.

Luxury home sales and prices in Washington ticked up this past quarter, Axios DC reports. But the broader homebuying market is softening: Redfin found that last month, sellers outnumbered buyers by 26% in D.C.





FROM VIRGINIA

Loudoun County, home to the world’s densest cluster of data centers, is the latest region to suggest hitting pause on new development while weighing how to regulate the industry, Virginia Business reports.

A $22.5 billion renovation of Dulles Airport, expected to be unveiled by President Donald Trump this week, will scrap the airport’s famous mobile lounge transportation system, CBS News reports. Plans include a major terminal expansion and a new underground aerotrain system.



PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


For the anime fan: Otakon at the Washington Convention Center, Friday.

For the mover and groover: The Funset at Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company, Friday.

For aspiring dancers: Maryland Youth Ballet’s “Sleeping Beauty" at Wolf Trap, Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

Nationals fans took a brief trip to the past on Monday as Max Scherzer — now sporting a Blue Jays uniform — made what could be his final start in Washington. As NOTUS’ Jesse Dougherty writes, the 42-year-old pitcher provided a reminder of what it means to care deeply about each game.

Are you ready for some football? The Commanders officially open training camp today. Fans will be allowed to attend 11 practices over the next month, including a joint session with the Dolphins on Aug. 12.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Blue Jays, 1:05 p.m. (MLB.TV)

NWSL: Spirit at Utah Royals, 9 p.m. (NWSL+)

entries.title: Signal Sent. Now What?
entries.content:
Today’s notice: What comes next after last night’s Senate vote. Slotkin weighs in on “Ogre-gate.” An uncomfortably timed pardon for Pennsylvania’s 7th. Wasserman Schultz’s redistricting problem. One woman’s quest to claw back Platner donations. And: federal workers vs. the EEOC. 





THE LATEST

The Senate sent a message: We stand with Ukraine. By a vote of 86-12 last night, the Senate advanced a Russia sanctions package that was in part a tribute to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who had long championed the issue, and in part a strong rebuke of a movement to dial back U.S. support for Ukraine in the country’s long war countering Vladimir Putin’s invasion.

The bill had languished before Graham’s death, NOTUS’ Joe Gould and Hamed Ahmadi write, but got moving again in part due to a provision added by Graham’s replacement — his sister, Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina). The new language would extend existing sanctions authority over Iran’s energy and weapons sectors through 2031, as demanded by Donald Trump.

Sanctions supporters say the cloture vote was all anyone needs to know about where the president stands now, despite his administration’s initial skepticism of ongoing support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian leader watched the vote from the Senate gallery last night, calling it “a big signal to Europe, a big signal to Ukraine, big support of our people.”

It’s still, though, just a signal. The bill still needs final passage in the Senate and in the House, which isn’t back until Aug. 31 and where the sanctions measure’s chances are less than assured.

Some Democrats see the bill as a shadow endorsement of Trump’s tariff powers. “I don’t know that we have much evidence that he’s going to use it to do what we need him to do,” said Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia), one of those 12 “no” votes.

Plenty of people from MAGAworld remain skeptical of Ukraine, and are not interested in continuing support for the war. Yesterday, however, Politico reported on Trump ally Laura Loomer’s conversion to a Ukraine backer. But that high-profile shift may not be enough.

“The idea that there’s been some sea change in opinion amongst the base as it relates to Ukraine isn’t accurate,” a Republican strategist close to the White House told NOTUS’ Jasmine Wright. “The Republican establishment has always had Zelenskyy’s back. Hopefully they’ll learn how to have America’s before November.”

Open tabs: Federal Immigration Agents Called Latinos Racial Slurs While Conducting Stops, Video Shows (NOTUS); Senate Confirms Jay Clayton as Director of National Intelligence (NOTUS); ICE Arrests Surge at Airports, Opening New Front in Deportation Drive (NYT); US thwarts Iranian missile attack and launches strikes with Saudi Arabia against militias in Iraq (AP)





From the campaign trail


Elissa Slotkin comes off the sidelines in the Michigan primary. “All leaders should be thoughtful about their language and not use language about hurting people,” the Democratic senator from Michigan told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic when asked about the recent “Ogre-gate” controversy in the hotly contested Senate primary between Rep. Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed. Slotkin is one of the few remaining Democratic electeds in the state not to take a side in the primary. Her language was couched but suggested she’s joining the chorus condemning El-Sayed for using the term, which some thought was aimed at Stevens. El-Sayed said it was actually about Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania).

Department of Awkward Timing. On June 30, Republican megadonor Adam Kidan, a key figure in the Jack Abramoff fraud and lobbying scandal, donated $2,600 to the leadership PAC for Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pennsylvania). On July 3, Trump pardoned Kidan, wiping away a guilty plea to fraud charges and likely vacating significant restitution payments. NOTUS’ Avani Kalra reports that Mackenzie’s office said the congressman didn’t talk to the White House or Trump about the pardon before it happened, and declined to say whether he’ll keep the campaign donation.

Mackenzie might have just been the last stop on the donation gravy train. Kidan has been a prolific donor this cycle, particularly in Pennsylvania, giving to GOP Reps. Rob Bresnahan, Brian Fitzpatrick and Scott Perry.

Scenes from redistricting: Florida’s 20th. “The greatest civil rights threat that’s facing us today” is how rapper Luther “Uncle Luke” Campbell, formerly of 2 Live Crew, described Democratic Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz’s decision to run in the Fort Lauderdale district. Campbell is one of several Black candidates running in the district’s Democratic primary, and has assailed the veteran white congresswoman for jumping into a district that, until state Republicans redrew the lines this year, was majority Black. NOTUS’ Oriana González reports on how fears of diluted Black political power are playing out in the primary.





THE BIG ONE

Refund, please! There’s an effort afoot to help Graham Platner donors recoup their money to the now defunct Maine campaign. The only question is whether those who gave money will actually do it.

Activist and lawyer Cheyenne Hunt is deploying her organization, Reckoning Action, to mass text the donors directly and walk them through how to get their money back, NOTUS’ Oriana González reports. It’s a move Hunt took after seeing former Rep. Eric Swalwell use campaign funds to pay legal fees after multiple sexual assault allegations.

Automated texts were sent with this message: “If you donated to Graham Platner and feel betrayed, you’re not alone. You signed up to help elect a champion for freedom and equality and take back the Senate — not to fund a predator.” FEC reports showed Platner had $1.7 million in cash on hand at the end of last month.





NOTUS METRO

NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter!

Sports desk: As Training Camp Begins, Commanders Say They Are ‘Happy’ With Receivers, by Martenzie Johnson






ON NOTUS PODCAST

From your favorite podcast app: On today’s episode of On NOTUS, Rep. Nanette Barragán (D-California) said Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 have “buyer’s remorse.” “They’re looking at what’s happening and saying, ‘This is not what we voted for,’” Barragán told NOTUS’ Oriana González. Barragán also talked about her vote to end all U.S. aid to Israel, the future of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus and her recruiting pitch to former MLB players to bolster the Democratic lineup in the Congressional Baseball Game.



NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

Last week’s arrival of a new season of “King of the Hill” is good news for America, says Matt K. Lewis, because the show is a roadmap to a better conservatism.







NEW ON NOTUS

EEOC pauses class actions by employees against federal agencies. That’s the allegation from a new lawsuit filed by the American Federation of Government Employees, which has asked a judge to compel the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to resume processing class-action complaints, NOTUS’ Eric Katz reports. The upshot of the pause is federal employees alleging sexual harassment or other forms of discrimination are currently blocked from collectively seeking relief, he writes.

The EEOC did not respond to a request for comment. Eric notes that Project 2025 suggested that the EEOC should no longer hear complaints from federal employees, and that those responsibilities should be transferred to the Merit Systems Protection Board.

entries.title: Former CHC Chair Nanette Barragán: Latino Trump Voters Have ‘Buyer’s Remorse’
entries.summary: The California Democrat says Trump misled Latino voters on the economy.
entries.content:
Rep. Nanette Barragán, the former chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, said Latinos who voted for President Trump in the 2024 election have “buyer’s remorse” over his promises on the economy and immigration.

“They’re saying, ‘I’m worse off, I’m paying more in higher cost, higher prices. I can't afford this anymore,’” Barragán said on the latest episode of the On NOTUS podcast. “‘We thought he was going to go after the worst of the worst, the criminals.’ He's not, he's going after our gardeners, our housekeepers, even doctors, DACA recipients.”

“They're looking at what's happening and saying, ‘This is not what we voted for,’” Barragán said.

According to the exit polls, Trump carried 46% of Hispanic and Latino voters in the 2024 election, up from 32% in the demographic in the 2020 election.

Barragán said that Democrats faltered with Latino voters in the 2024 election because of a failure in communication.

“I think Democrats got so much done that we didn't know what to focus on,” Barragán said. “People were not feeling what we did. And a lot of this is how people feel. … If they don't feel it, they're not going to give us credit. They're going to try something else.”

Barragán said it was “unfortunate” that sitting Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chair Adriano Espaillat lost his primary to Darializa Avila Chevalier, but she believes it was likely due to the New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s endorsement of Chevalier rather than the weakness of the CHC.

“I don't know the politics of New York, but I know one thing, and that is the mayor there has been popular,” Barragán said. “His messaging is resonating with a lot of Americans.”

Chevalier expressed interest in joining the Hispanic Caucus if she’s elected in November — Barragán said she expects Chevalier to be approved by an admission vote of the members.

With more self-proclaimed socialists expected to join her in Congress, Barragán said she does not know what values socialists stand for but that Democrats of all stripes were united to oppose President Trump.

“My understanding is whether you're a Democrat or you're a democratic socialist, you don't agree with this president and what he's doing on raising costs,” Barragán said. “I believe we should be welcoming of anybody, even if Republicans want to make the switch.”

Barragán was one of more than 100 House Democrats who voted yes on an amendment from Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to end all aid to Israel.

The California Democrat said the amendment was “overbroad” and cut necessary humanitarian aid, but defended her vote as the will of her constituents.

“At the end of the day, it was about listening to constituents and also sending a message that we are not going to continue to support [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's wars and the killing of innocent people with our money,” Barragán said. “Just like I vote against President Trump and his money for war, it's the same rationale.”

Barragán supported a measure to send military aid to Israel in 2024, but said Netanyahu’s leadership led her to change her stance.

“Things have changed, the landscape has changed,” Barragán said. “It was time to say we're not just going to keep funding something because we've done it in the past. We're going to look at everything going on, and we're not going to support a president in Israel who is just frankly doing whatever he wants.”

entries.title: ACLU Seeks Government Payouts for Immigration Agent Misconduct
entries.summary: “I'm an ordinary woman, and I want to stand up,” one of the ACLU clients said.
entries.content:
American Civil Liberties Union affiliates across the country said they filed 30 claims this week seeking damages for the wrongdoing of federal agents involved in immigration enforcement.

The litigation effort announced Wednesday includes 54 claims filed since February in 17 states and Washington, D.C. The claims include allegations of abuses in immigration detention, attacks against people exercising First Amendment rights, racial profiling and unlawful arrests of U.S. citizens and immigrants.

The ACLU said it seeks to hold federal immigration agents accountable via the Federal Torts Claim Act, a 1946 statute that allows people to get compensation for federal employees’ misconduct. But attorneys face multiple hurdles and yearslong battles before the possibility of a settlement or bench trial.

“We are filing these coordinated claims for the clients to have a path for accountability, to be able to show and demonstrate the harms that they have endured, and to have redress for that,” Yasmin Cader, an ACLU deputy executive director, said. “But it is also really important that we expose the abuse, and that we elevate the human toll of the Trump's administration's brutal enforcement practices.”

Willy Wender Aceituno and Norma Bowe are two of the clients ACLU affiliates are representing.

Immigration agents twice stopped and detained Aceituno, a U.S. citizen, on Nov. 15 in Charlotte, North Carolina, according to a notice of the claims sent to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection.

The agents shattered his car window, which resulted in cuts, and took him in an SUV for 15 minutes, releasing him after confirming his citizenship. His detention caused physical, emotional, and psychological harm, the notice says.

Bowe, a 68-year-old professor of public health at Kean University and registered nurse, brought forward a claim this week that says ICE officers outside of the Delaney Hall detention center threw her to the ground on May 25.

The nurse, who operates an RV clinic outside the New Jersey detention center, argues that at the time she was trying to help a woman protesting whose shirt had ripped. Bowe says she still has doctors’ appointments related to the injuries from hitting the pavement.

Acetituno is seeking $1.2 million in damages and Bowe is seeking $500,000.

“I'm an ordinary woman, and I want to stand up,” Bowe told NOTUS. “I want people to know my story, and I'm hoping that it will help other folks also stand up with their story.”

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, asked how many claims ICE and CBP have received since January 2025, said agents will continue to arrest the “worst of the worst” immigrants who are illegally present in the U.S., no matter how many lawsuits are filed.

“FTCA claims remain under review. Agitators who obstruct or assault federal law enforcement officers will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” the spokesperson said in an email.

To bring forward an FTCA claim, the person who suffered the injury has to do so within two years and wait six months for the agency employing the federal worker to respond, according to a congressional research report. If the agency denies the claim or doesn’t respond, the claimant can move forward with a federal lawsuit.

Before Congress enacted the FTCA, the only way to obtain compensation for federal employees’ wrongful actions was to petition lawmakers to pass a bill. “That was a horrible system,” said Paul Figley, a law professor who was the deputy director of the Justice Department’s FTCA division for 15 years.

Figley said immigration-enforcement-related claims are difficult and that the factual details of each case, rather than the policies of the Trump administration, would matter to reach a successful outcome for the ACLU.

And he warned these cases could become too political and attempt to curb the administration’s policy-making decisions, which wasn’t Congress’ intention with the statute.

“The FTCA isn't there to provide a remedy for everybody that's been hurt,” Figley said. “It's there to provide a remedy for run-of-the-mill, everyday kinds of things that don't affect how the government's operating.”

Cases arising from President Donald Trump’s second term might not be solved until the next administration. For example, a federal court approved a $435,000 total settlement in March for four undocumented mothers whom Border Patrol agents expelled to Mexico days after giving birth in 2020, according to court documents.

The National Immigration Litigation Alliance and the law office of Bardis Vakili represented the mothers in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California.

NILA was also part of the legal team that obtained a $1.4 million settlement for a group of mothers and their children separated under the first Trump administration’s “zero tolerance” policy. Their lawsuit was filed in 2019 and the court approved the settlement in 2024. Fathers and their children got $1.9 million in a similar lawsuit.

“If the government injures an individual, that individual should be compensated for that injury, if it was an unlawful injury,” Mary Kenney, NILA’s deputy director, said. “And our client population can use the money.”

entries.title: Trump Teleprompter Operator at Center of Gambling Scandal Is Out of a Job
entries.summary: Gabriel Perez, who allegedly made roughly $100,000 betting on Trump’s speeches, was previously placed on unpaid leave.
entries.content:
The teleprompter operator accused of unlawfully gambling on President Donald Trump’s speeches via a prediction marketplace is no longer employed by the White House.

A White House official confirmed Wednesday that Gabriel Perez “no longer works in the federal government.”

It is unclear whether the White House fired Perez or if he resigned.

Perez allegedly placed bets on Kalshi that were flagged by the company’s surveillance team to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, according to Robert DeNault, the head of enforcement for Kalshi.

“We have charged this individual and have been assisting regulators on this matter and provided evidence we collected, as we do in any referral,” DeNault said in a statement earlier this month.

Perez, who is accused of making roughly $100,000 from the bets, has cooperated with federal investigators from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a source familiar with the matter previously told NOTUS.

Trump called the incident “deeply unfortunate,” White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said during a briefing on July 16. At the time, Perez had been placed on unpaid leave.

Leavitt previously told NOTUS that no other White House staff are currently suspected of misconduct related to wagering on prediction markets.

Lawmakers from both parties have advocated for legislation to prohibit federal elected officials and government employees from using insider information to place bets on prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket. In April, the Justice Department alleged that U.S. Army Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke, who was involved in the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, used classified information to place a wager on Polymarket.

entries.title: Fauci Repeatedly Invokes the Fifth at Rand Paul’s COVID Hearing
entries.summary: In his opening statement, Fauci told the committee that he believed Paul had an “unhinged obsession” with jailing him.
entries.content:
Former infectious disease official Anthony Fauci refused to answer questions in a contentious Wednesday morning hearing held by his outspoken critic, Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, repeatedly invoking the Fifth Amendment.

In his opening statement, Fauci told the Senate Committee on Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs that he believed Paul had an “unhinged obsession” with jailing him, and the only reason he was holding the hearing was to try to catch Fauci in a lie.

“Therefore, although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said.

Despite the witness’s lack of cooperation, Paul proceeded with questioning Fauci. The senator has long pushed theories that the COVID-19 virus emerged from a lab in China, and that Fauci was aware of this — and knowingly funding risky infectious disease work at the Chinese lab in question. Most scientists agree that the pandemic originated from a natural source, probably a wild animal.

As promised, Fauci refused to answer any questions.

“On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution,” he said repeatedly in his light Brooklyn drawl.

At one point, Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, attempted to address the committee. Paul had security remove him from the hearing room. Many members of the audience applauded his removal as he left.

In a written statement provided to NOTUS, Schertler said that the circumstances surrounding the hearing, including Paul’s repeated calls for Fauci’s imprisonment and the “foreseeable result of these outlandish statements” — including harassment and death threats towards Fauci and members of his family — “regrettably made his continued cooperation impossible.”

“The accusations that Chairman Paul continues to propagate are false and disgraceful, and we will examine all options to hold him accountable,” Schertler said in the statement.

Paul told Fauci the committee would have to consider “what appropriate action” to take after the hearing in response to his refusal to answer questions.

“There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today,” Paul told Fauci. “It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress.”

Courts have previously upheld a witness’s right to invoke the Fifth Amendment in response to a congressional subpoena if they fear self-incrimination. In recent history, the former CEO of ActBlue and a former Biden aide have also declined to answer questions in hearings.

Paul and others who opposed the federal government’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic have repeatedly called for Fauci’s imprisonment. In response, former President Joe Biden issued Fauci a preemptive pardon before leaving office.

Paul’s frustration with Fauci was apparent even before the former health official revealed his strategy.

“Frankly, the American people deserve an apology,” Paul told Fauci in his opening statement as chair of the committee.

“That loss of trust may be your most damaging legacy,” Paul said, speaking from a teleprompter. Fauci led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases from 1984 until 2022 and played a key role in the global fight against AIDS as well as COVID-19.

The hearing took place in one of the smaller Senate hearing rooms. Many of the seats were reserved for guests of Paul’s committee. Included in the audience was Mary Holland, CEO of Children’s Health Defense, a vaccine-skeptical organization formerly led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“Ladies and gentlemen, I’m going to have to ask you to put two masks on,” a man sitting in a committee-reserved seat said jokingly to his neighbors before the hearing began.

It’s the culmination of a frenetic week for both Paul and Fauci. On Tuesday, Paul published excerpts from Fauci’s diary from the pandemic years, claiming that he orchestrated a cover-up of the fact that the pandemic originated in a lab and was the result of so-called “gain-of-function” research, or laboratory work on infectious diseases that makes them more dangerous to humans.

Soon after the release of the diary excerpts, the Trump administration released new guidance prohibiting federal funding going to what it deems gain-of-function research. Scientists have raised concerns that overly broad restrictions could disrupt important research into infectious diseases.

Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin), another Fauci critic, attempted to question Fauci on whether the pulmonary infarction he wrote about in the released diary could have been caused by the COVID-19 vaccine. Johnson has repeatedly claimed that the federal government suppressed evidence of dangerous side effects caused by the vaccine.

In contrast to Paul’s threats of repercussions, one Republican appeared to affirm Fauci’s right to decline to answer questions. Like Paul, Sen. James Lankford (R-Oklahoma) attempted to question Fauci on whether the virus originated from a lab. But Lankford responded, “as is your right to do,” when Fauci invoked his right to not answer the question.

Democrats on the committee apologized to Fauci for his being compelled to appear.

“We are here in an attempt to entrap you,” Sen. Margaret Wood Hassan (D-New Hampshire) said during her questioning period, in which she did not actually ask Fauci any questions.

Gary Peters (D-Michigan), the ranking member of the committee, accused Paul of ignoring the actual duties of the committee in favor of promoting his theories around COVID-19.

He pointed to cuts to the public health agencies as the more pressing issue at hand.

“Instead of focusing on the national security challenges that we are facing in our country right now, today’s hearing looks backwards, revisiting questions this committee has already examined,” Peters said. “History tells us, unfortunately, another pandemic is all but inevitable. The question is whether Congress and this committee will work to better prepare our country for it, or continue looking backward while our public health infrastructure crumbles around us.”

entries.title: Fed Maintains Interest Rates as Trump Escalates His Threats Against Iran
entries.summary: The committee cited “elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East.”
entries.content:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday as Chair Kevin Warsh and Fed officials contend with volatile oil prices and persistent inflation since the pandemic.

“Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East,” the Federal Open Market Committee said in a statement.

The Fed has now cited the conflict in the Middle East for contributing to economic uncertainty in four consecutive decisions to keep interest rates where they are.

That hasn’t stopped President Donald Trump — who told Fox News Wednesday morning that the U.S. would “beat the fucking shit out” of Iran — from insisting on lower rates.

Trump accused board members of standing in the way of lower rates, in a gaggle with reporters Monday.

“Kevin’s fantastic, but he’s got a board, and the board members are very political,” Trump said. “You need the consent of some people that have perhaps bad intentions.”

The Fed’s rate-setting committee voted 9-3 to preserve rates at 3.5 to 3.75% for the fifth consecutive meeting since December, citing elevated inflation stemming in part from energy prices and strong productivity growth and capital investment.

The three officials in the minority voted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point. Officials indicated in their quarterly projections last month — a practice that Warsh has criticized for revealing too much of the central bank’s thinking to eager investors — that rates may rise this year to tamp down inflation.

Warsh is being pulled in opposite directions by high inflation numbers and a president who has made no secret that he wants to see rates slashed to stimulate economic growth. The annual inflation rate slowed from 4.2% in May to 3.5% in June as the U.S. and Iran settled into a ceasefire agreement, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The rate-setting committee maintains a goal of lowering inflation to 2%. The inflation rate last punched in at or below 2% in February 2021.

That goal increasingly appears far away for the central bank. Oil prices surged this month after Trump announced the end of the ceasefire with Iran on July 8.

Warsh has his own qualms with Fed officials.

The Fed chair wants to transform how the Fed communicates with the public. He has criticized officials’ “dot plot” economic projections and the practice of Fed governors delivering speeches on economic topics around the country. Warsh has also shortened interest rate announcements from the FOMC, saying markets are overly sensitive to Fed communications.

Warsh recently appointed five task forces that will examine topics ranging from Fed communications to the impact of AI on the economy and the drivers of inflation. The members include university economists, former foreign central bankers and CEOs.

entries.title: James Comey Accuses DOJ of Lying and ‘Vindictive’ Prosecution in Seashell Case
entries.summary: The former FBI director’s lawyers seek to suppress evidence and dismiss the indictment over an “86 47” social media post.
entries.content:
Attorneys for former FBI director James Comey accused Justice Department officials of misleading judges, omitting key facts and making false statements in their case charging him with threatening to kill President Donald Trump via a social media post.

In three court filings late Tuesday, Comey’s lawyers also argued the Justice Department had improperly singled out Comey for prosecution because Trump was upset that Comey had publicly criticized him.

The motions – hundreds of pages in all – attacked a central theory in the government’s case and sought to suppress some evidence, allow Comey’s attorneys to review grand jury transcripts and dismiss the indictment as a vindictive and selective prosecution.

The indictment “is not based on a good faith application of the law to the facts,” Comey’s lawyers wrote in one of the motions. “Instead, it effectuates a yearslong campaign by the President to use the criminal process to punish Mr. Comey for his protected speech and because of the President’s deep-seated animosity.”

The filings are the second this week from Comey’s legal team and represent a sweeping attempt to cut short a case that Trump’s critics say is emblematic of the president’s retribution agenda. In a separate motion on Monday, Comey asked the judge overseeing the case to throw out the charges, arguing his post did not constitute a true threat.

A White House spokesperson referred questions about the case to the Justice Department, which doesn’t typically discuss pending cases. A Justice Department spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.

Comey’s lawyers zeroed in on the extensive efforts federal investigators made over nearly a year to turn up evidence that Comey intended to threaten Trump’s life when he uploaded a photo to Instagram of seashells spelling “86 47.”

Echoing claims from Trump’s allies that the slogan was a call to violence, prosecutors alleged that “86” had roots in organized crime as jargon for “kill” and that Comey would have known this from his time investigating and prosecuting mobsters. They say the “47” represents Trump as the 47th president.

But Comey’s lawyers said investigators found no such connection, despite spending months combing through case files and organized-crime trial transcripts and interviewing experts to substantiate the theory.

“Those efforts, which preceded the government’s applications for the warrants, failed to find any evidence proving that Mr. Comey learned that ‘86’ means ‘kill’ in the organized crime context — because it does not,” the lawyers wrote.

The FBI case agent who applied for the warrants, which sought records from Apple ID and Gmail accounts associated with Comey and his wife, Patrice Comey, made no mention of investigators’ failed searches, despite having personally ordered it, according to the filings.

The omission, Comey’s lawyers said, “is all the more egregious because all of those investigations supported Mr. Comey’s assertion that he did not recall ever hearing ‘86’ used to mean ‘kill’ during his prosecutorial days.”

Comey’s filings include a blistering sworn statement from John Gleeson, a former federal prosecutor and judge in Brooklyn who tried crime boss John Gotti. He said he’d never heard a mafia member use the term “86,” nor had it come up in reference to killing in his thousands of hours of conversations with mafia witnesses.

“The claim that ‘86’ is mafia jargon for ‘kill’ is preposterous,” Gleeson wrote. “In my expert opinion, there is literally no support for the central allegation on which the case rests.”

Comey’s lawyers also said the Justice Department had “distorted” statements from an unidentified associate of the Comeys who spoke with Secret Service and FBI agents. The affidavits claimed that the person “immediately” thought “86” could have been a call to violence, when in fact the person told investigators that they initially viewed the term as benign restaurant lingo, according to the lawyers.

The person had no insight into Comey’s mental state, having not spoken to him in two years, and had been exposed to a false claim that “86” had been used to indicate violence in cases Comey had prosecuted, according to the filings. And the person had told investigators that they hoped Comey “goes to jail” and described their views about Comey as “speculation,” his lawyers said.

“These inconvenient facts — all disproving the government’s central theory, and all known to the agent who sought the warrants — appeared nowhere in the affidavits seeking to obtain the private digital records of Mr. Comey and his wife,” his lawyers wrote.

The lawyers also targeted what they said was a false implication in one of the warrants that one of Comey’s lawyers had obstructed the investigation.

The lawyer, a former federal prosecutor, had sent a screenshot of the seashell photo to a Secret Service agent who informally requested it, according to the filing. The FBI’s search warrant affidavit suggested that the lawyer had tried to conceal evidence in doing so, even though the agent had never asked for the original file.

Comey’s lawyers are seeking what’s known as a Franks hearing, in which a judge determines whether investigators lied or left out important facts to secure a search warrant.

In a separate motion, his lawyers asked the court to force the government to turn over grand jury transcripts and audio recordings. They said the government’s alleged omissions and false statements raised “a significant risk that irregularities in the grand jury process influenced the grand jury to return an indictment.”

Comey’s lawyers also argued that the case should be thrown out because the Justice Department’s prosecution was “vindictive,” “selective,” and designed to retaliate against Comey for publicly criticizing the president.

Vindictive prosecution is a legal doctrine in which a prosecutor improperly charges a person in retaliation for exercising legal rights such as free speech. Selective prosecution occurs when a prosecutor targets a person with charges that haven’t been brought against people who did the same thing in similar situations.

Both practices are unconstitutional and represent serious prosecutorial misconduct, but they are difficult to prove in court. Federal judges have recognized broad discretion in how prosecutors bring cases, and defendants who raise vindictive or selective prosecution claims rarely prevail.

This is Comey’s second indictment by Trump’s Justice Department. Under heavy pressure from Trump, prosecutors in Virginia charged Comey last fall with lying to Congress. That case stemmed from his 2020 congressional testimony about alleged leaks to journalists related to FBI investigations of Trump and Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaigns.

Comey had argued vindictive and selective prosecution in that case, but a judge dismissed the case on the grounds that the lead prosecutor, White House appointee Lindsey Halligan, had no authority to bring the charges.

Frustrated by the failed indictment and the pace of other prosecutions of high-profile figures, Trump in April fired then-attorney general Pam Bondi and allowed her deputy, Todd Blanche, to assume the role on an acting basis.

Under Blanche, who served as Trump’s criminal lawyer between presidencies, the Justice Department indicted Comey again in North Carolina, this time on counts of threats against the president and making threats across state lines. Several weeks after the new indictment was filed, Trump nominated Blanche to be attorney general.

When Comey posted the “86 47” image last year, many of Trump’s allies claimed it was a call for the president’s murder. Comey denied he had any violent intent, saying the message was political, and quickly deleted the post. Secret Service agents interviewed him in Washington shortly after.

Comey’s lawyers said in their filing Monday that “86 47” has become a well known and widely used political slogan expressing opposition to Trump with no significant violent connotations.

The government’s claim of a “true threat,” they wrote, “is contradicted by every possible source of meaning: dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense.”
