entries.title: Trump Administration Wants Millions More to Pay Off Freedom 250 Events
entries.summary: “It is unacceptable to ask the American people to bail out Freedom 250,” Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley said of the request.
entries.content:
The Interior Department is seeking $10 million in additional funding from Congress for previously held events hosted by Freedom 250, Sen. Jeff Merkley revealed in a letter sent to Secretary Doug Burgum Wednesday.

In the letter, Merkley (D-Oregon) said the Interior Department is seeking the money to reimburse the National Park Service for its work during the Rededicate 250 prayer event, the Great American State Fair, and the July 4th Salute to America event. All were hosted by Freedom 250, the public-private partnership founded by the Trump administration to plan events in celebration of America’s 250th birthday. The task force effectively sidelined America 250, the bipartisan, congressionally mandated organization formed for the same purpose.

Merkley, who is the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations subcommittee that oversees funding for the Interior Department, asked Burgum to respond to the letter by Aug. 7 with a full accounting of how NPS has spent the $150 million provided in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” for semiquincentennial events and activities.

“It is unacceptable to ask the American people to bail out Freedom 250. Congress already appropriated $150 million—without bipartisan input—with the administration promising that private donors would help finance the rest. If the administration designated Freedom 250 as the responsible entity for these events, Freedom 250—not taxpayers—should be paying the remaining costs,” Merkley wrote.

He said that Interior Department staff also held a closed-door briefing with senators that failed to elicit answers to his questions about where, exactly, the additional money would go.

“Our understanding from the administration was that taxpayer funds would contribute $150 million and private donations would contribute the balance of the funding,” Merkley wrote. “Given that understanding, what has gone wrong that has led to this additional request for taxpayer funds?”

The Interior Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NOTUS, but told The Washington Post on Wednesday that the extra funding was needed to help address security needs, citing recent threats at the White House correspondents’ dinner and the UFC event held on the White House lawn.

“Given the elevated security threats against high-profile events in Washington, D.C. … an elevated security posture was needed to ensure the safety of the public at these events. This funding would help address the expenditures associated with the elevated security posture,” a spokesperson for the department said.

entries.title: Iran-Focused U.S.-Israel Meeting Sidelines Allies’ Other Disagreements
entries.summary: Despite growing fears over Israel’s policies in Lebanon and the Palestinian territories, Trump and Netanyahu put a positive spin on their brief meeting.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu put a positive spin on their Tuesday meeting, which Trump called “very good” and Netanyahu deemed “excellent.” But the summit did little to resolve central issues in the U.S.-Israel relationship — suggesting disagreements between the allies and unprecedented skepticism of Tel Aviv among the American public are likely to continue.

On its surface, the summit addressed the Iran war, which Trump launched in partnership with Netanyahu and neither has been able to resolve, despite its rising toll for Americans, regional security and the global economy. Netanyahu said the countries share the goal of preventing Iranian development of nuclear weapons (an objective Iran denies having) and Trump on Wednesday issued a fresh threat toward Tehran after an Iranian missile attack on U.S. forces in Jordan. Trump has suggested Netanyahu should be more deferential toward the U.S., and before the Israeli leader arrived in Washington, his government finally approved a step forward for Trump’s plan for the Gaza Strip, allowing foreign troops to enter a small part of the territory.

The development regarding Gaza encapsulated the general mood: little headway in areas where stated U.S. and Israeli preferences diverge. Israel slashed the number of forces permitted and maintains it must continue controlling nearly 70% of the Palestinian territory, though Trump has spoken of Israeli withdrawal.

Tuesday’s meeting “was a meeting Trump preferred not to have, but was ultimately pressured into,” Eran Etzion, a long-time Israeli diplomat and former deputy head of the country’s national security council, told NOTUS. Netanyahu was visiting town for the first time since the Iran war began, for the funeral of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina.

Etzion argued the White House summit seemed designed to avoid tough conversations about simmering tensions.

“It was orchestrated to minimize both media exposure and one-on-one face time. The number of attendees was bloated, which probably means sensitive issues were off the table,” said Etzion, who is now seeking a seat in Israel’s parliament as a member of the Democrats party, a rival to Netanyahu.

A spokesperson for the Israeli Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, Israeli policies that have fueled a backlash among Americans and complicated Trump administration gambits, like attempted diplomacy with Iran and a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia, are intensifying.

U.S. sentiment toward Israel has cratered over the country’s devastating American-backed offensive in Gaza since 2023. An Economist/YouGov poll conducted July 27-29 shows 43% of Americans (including 22% of Trump voters) now say the policy constitutes a genocide. Nearly 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since a Trump-enforced ceasefire in October, according to Palestinian authorities, and millions more still face Israeli attacks. And relief groups say Israel continues to sharply restrict the flow of humanitarian aid. In Gaza, 67% of residents are at a crisis level or worse of food insecurity, the United Nations-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification monitor said this month, and chickenpox has begun rapidly spreading in overcrowded camps of displaced Palestinians.

Rebuilding the strip — part of the mission of Trump’s Board of Peace — would require over $71 billion, more than seven times the cost of reconstruction following past Israeli campaigns, Oxfam, the Palestine Economic Policy Research Institute and the Palestine Trade Center said in a July 22 report.

Meanwhile, concerns from human rights groups and U.S. lawmakers are ongoing about people from Gaza who Israel has detained and is accused of torturing, like Hussam Abu Safiya, a former head of a hospital who has been held since December 2024. Diana Buttu, an analyst and former peace negotiator who is monitoring Abu Safiya’s case, told NOTUS there have been no updates despite growing international calls for his release this summer following suggestions he may be on the brink of death. Broadly, for detained Palestinians, “nobody is held to account” within Israel’s system, Buttu said. (Israel denies mistreating Palestinian detainees.)

In the West Bank, the other Palestinian territory occupied by Israel under international law, increased violence by Israeli settlers close to Netanyahu’s far-right political partners and government moves targeting Palestinian families have spurred fears of a major conflagration.

Ahead of Netanyahu’s U.S. visit, several hundred former senior officials in Israel's national security forces signed a letter asking Trump to pressure Netanyahu to limit “Jewish terror.” Among those targeted by orders disrupting Palestinian life is, Buttu said, a family of 14 in a village called Umm al-Khair who can no longer access their own bathroom because it has been deemed a “closed military zone.”

Together, the trajectory is a far cry from Trump’s talk of delivering Israeli-Palestinian peace and progress for the Middle East. For the president, that has broader ramifications. He has tied his marquee effort to sell American nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia to Saudi recognition of Israel. But Saudi officials and those close to them continue to reiterate that is impossible without concrete action toward establishing Palestinian statehood.

Beyond Israel-Palestine, a conflict and humanitarian crisis are ongoing in Lebanon — and Iran has said developments in that country are crucial to any U.S.-Iranian diplomacy.

Israeli forces control much of the country’s south, enforcing what Buttu, who recently visited the Israeli side of the border, called “Gazafication” by demolishing homes and communities. Israel says its campaign is necessary to deter the Iran-backed Lebanese militia Hezbollah.

The U.S. is promoting the idea that Lebanon’s government and military will disarm Hezbollah. Continued Israeli occupation undermines their authority to do so, analysts say — and Trump has declined to deploy American pressure over Netanyahu for a withdrawal.

With a settlement over Lebanon stalled and signs of fresh escalations, there’s no end in sight for the Iran war. In turn, there’s little chance of addressing the frustration with Netanyahu and with Trump for launching that conflict that has grown nationally, including among conservatives who are seeking a U.S.-Israel reset.

entries.title: Trump Administration Announces Another Data Center on Federal Land
entries.summary: The Energy Department is partnering with developers and utilities to build an artificial intelligence “innovation campus” in Kentucky.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is accelerating its push to build data centers on federally controlled land — allowing developers and utility companies to sidestep permitting battles and community backlash.

The Energy Department announced Wednesday it is partnering with NextEra Energy, Brookfield and three utilities to build an “artificial intelligence and high-performance computing innovation campus” on portions of DOE’s Paducah Site in western Kentucky, which was built in the 1950s to enrich uranium.

The plans include 2 gigawatts of new natural gas-fired power generation and more than 2½ gigawatts of battery storage. That’s more power than the data center is expected to need, which would allow the generators to deliver power to nearby homes and businesses, according to DOE.

Building data centers on federal sites has been a main goal of the Trump administration’s push to accelerate the pace of AI development. Last year, DOE offered up sites in Idaho, South Carolina, Tennessee and Kentucky for data center developers.

Another project on federal land, a combination of gas generators and a 10-gigawatt data center, was announced in southern Ohio this year. Federal officials are leasing land to SB Energy for that project, which DOE is branding as the world’s largest AI data center.

Energy officials say data centers can be constructed more quickly on federal sites, using fast-tracked permitting processes.

Building a data center on an existing DOE site comes with other advantages, too. Many of them are already set up with costly transmission infrastructure, previously used for Cold War-era nuclear enrichment facilities, to support national laboratories or for other energy-intensive programs.

Developers will also probably face fewer environmental hurdles, because many of these sites — especially those still undergoing nuclear cleanup — are already experiencing environmental degradation.

Those sites allow data center developers to avoid the major stumbling blocks that many other recent projects have faced: fierce local opposition and zoning and permitting issues.

The administration is attempting to help private companies build data centers on public lands as well, but facing bigger roadblocks. Developers must obtain a right-of-way on public lands, a process that involves additional evaluations and obligations to prevent environmental harm. The more complicated process means more chances for outside groups to stop the efforts: A plan to build a center on federal lands in Nevada is currently facing legal pushback from national environmental groups and local residents.

Michigan Democratic Rep. Rashida Tlaib has introduced a bill to ban AI data centers on all lands owned or managed by the federal government, citing the concerns of pollution and increased energy costs.

Rep. Andy Barr (R-Kentucky) called the new project in his state “historic” and said he personally advocated for the development.

“Together with our private sector partners, this investment will create jobs, strengthen our energy security, and deliver lasting economic growth for Paducah and the Commonwealth for decades to come,” he said.

The development will involve more than $100 billion in private investment, federal officials said, and create 8,000 construction jobs and 600 permanent jobs.

entries.title: Blanche Committee Vote in Limbo After Cornyn Meeting Canceled
entries.summary: “Maybe they think I’m just going to give up or go along, but they’re mistaken,” Cornyn said.
entries.content:
Sen. John Cornyn’s planned meeting on Wednesday with acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was canceled, imperiling the chances of his nomination advancing through the Judiciary Committee this week.

The Texas Republican said he was "disappointed" to have to cancel the meeting due to the Department of Justice’s unwillingness to produce an ironclad change to the IRS settlement that spawned a proposed $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund and shielded President Donald Trump from future tax audits. The DOJ did not return a request for comment.

The canceled meeting was slated to take place a day before the committee was scheduled to vote on Blanche’s nomination. Cornyn said that Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) wants an answer on how he will vote by 4 p.m. in case they need to postpone the markup. At this point, Cornyn remains an impediment.

“I’m not prepared to vote ‘yes,’ let me put it that way,” Cornyn said when asked if he planned to vote “no” on Thursday.

“Maybe they think I’m just going to give up or go along, but they’re mistaken,” Cornyn said of the DOJ’s lack of action on the fund.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina), another Judiciary Committee member, is aligned with Cornyn on what he needs to see from Blanche in order to support the nomination.

“I think they realize now that we’re serious. I think [Sen. Thom Tillis] is pretty much on the same page that I am. They better get real. There’s not much time left,” Cornyn said.

A “no” vote by either Cornyn or Tillis would likely doom Blanche’s chances of getting confirmed as attorney general.

“We’ve still got another five to six hours. That’s plenty of time to resolve this,” Cornyn continued. “There’s no real need to have a meeting if they produce the documentation that we requested and that he testified to under oath in his hearing.”

Cornyn has insisted that Blanche put in writing that the anti-weaponization fund will not go forward and that Blanche’s word that it is “dead” is insufficient. The Texas senator has noted repeatedly that the deal could be revived later via a breach of contract lawsuit, meaning that a change must be made in writing.

“I haven’t seen a single piece of writing that is responsive to what I requested. … There’s been a lot of back and forth with my staff. I don’t know if it’s been the reluctance of the DOJ staff," he said.

Republicans have been hoping to confirm Blanche next week before they depart for the Senate’s annual August recess.

entries.title: Trump Promises Iran Would ‘Get a Beating’ After Attack on U.S. Forces
entries.summary: The president delivered profanity-laced threats after a ballistic missile attack was intercepted in Jordan overnight.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump plans to retaliate against Iran after a ballistic missile attack on U.S. forces in the region was intercepted, telling Fox News on Wednesday that the U.S. will “beat the fucking shit out of them.”

The attack occurred overnight in Jordan, according to Iranian state media.

Trump said that the U.S. would be “hitting them hard. They’re going to get a beating.”

The White House declined to comment further, and the Pentagon did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The attack and pledge to respond came after Trump met on Tuesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to discuss the ongoing war against Iran. Though Netanyahu helped convince Trump to go to war with Iran in February and has sought continued aggression from U.S. forces, his relationship with the president had been under strain as it dragged on, increasing political pressure on Trump.

In a Truth Social post on Tuesday, Trump called his sitdown with Netanyahu “a very good meeting.”

Iran said on Wednesday that the intercepted attack targeted an American military base in Jordan, after U.S.-Saudi joint forces struck Iranian-allied forces in Iraq. Jordan’s military said it intercepted five missiles.

The U.S.-Saudi forces struck Iran-backed “logistics and weapons sites,” according to U.S. Central Command, hitting the Popular Mobilization Forces. The PMF said at least 20 people were killed in the attack.

Although Trump has sought an exit from the war for some time, the overnight action marked an escalation with Saudi Arabia’s entry into the fighting. The U.S. conducted airstrikes against Iran last week but had seemingly paused the attacks after military leaders reportedly warned against escalating further.

There are growing concerns over the military’s depleted stockpile of advanced air defense missiles. Experts have estimated the remaining number of Patriot interceptors in the U.S. arsenal to be around 827, with only 278 THAAD ballistic missile interceptors remaining, according to a report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies. But the president said last week in Georgia that Iran wasn’t ready for a peace deal.

“They want to make a deal, but I say they’re not ready to make a deal,” Trump said. “They’re not ready. They’ll be ready very soon.”

entries.title: Immigration Agents Bristled at ‘Stunt’ Operation Outside Newsom Rally, Texts Show
entries.summary: “Hopefully I can get replaced soon,” one agent groused after the incident.
entries.content:
Federal immigration agents privately bristled at their participation in a controversial operation outside of a press conference held by California Gov. Gavin Newsom in August 2025, text message screenshots filed in federal court this week revealed.

Two agents discussed the event — as well as their anxiety over the possibility of violating court orders — in messages that were among the exhibits submitted Monday by the American Civil Liberties Union in a California federal court. The exhibits also contained numerous incidents of federal immigration agents using crude and racist language toward Latinos.

Federal personnel from Border Patrol, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other agencies conducted widespread raids in Los Angeles last summer under Operation At Large, part of the Trump administration’s aggressive mass-deportation push.

The texts between the unidentified federal agents — one of whom was recognized in court documents as a Homeland Security Investigations special agent, referred to as Agent G.A. in the filings — offer a candid look into how agents privately viewed their roles in Operation At Large. The agent conversed with their colleague, or Agent W, in redacted records.

The incident in question occurred when Gregory Bovino, a polarizing former Border Patrol commander who was placed in charge of the Los Angeles operation, appeared with armed federal agents outside a museum in Los Angeles’ Little Tokyo neighborhood on Aug. 14, 2025, where Newsom was hosting a press conference for a redistricting proposition. The agents detained several people and lingered at the scene, sparking a flurry of media coverage.

At the time, DHS contended that the operation was about “enforcing the law.”
Screenshot 2026-07-28 at 7.46.08 PM.png (1784x1156, AR: 1.54)Newsom said in a social media post Wednesday that the released texts prove that the operation was targeted. The governor’s office referred to the posts when asked for comment.

“This is crazy. I never thought I would actually see anything like this. We got pulled off the HD and car wash to run this stunt,” Agent G.A. wrote that day, referencing sites such as Home Depot where agents would often appear to arrest day laborers and other workers.

The agent claimed they were told to “stand down” while at the press conference.

“We’re told to assist with targeted enforcement,” Agent G.A. wrote. “That is not target enforcement. That was just a political agenda. Hopefully I can get replaced soon.”

Agent G.A. wrote to Agent W again on Aug. 15, “I had no interest in going out with BP to Little Tokyo lol.” They said agents just “stood around to get media attention” after marching from a federal building in downtown LA to Newsom’s press conference and arresting a few people.

“Would you have went?” Agent G.A. asked.

“If I knew what they were doing probably not,” Agent W responded.
https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/2082544247832735976?s=20Agent W brought up Bovino, saying they had heard he was a “good dude and really good at his job” but at times did “things like this that are a little out of pocket.”

“I think BP is mostly just excited because they don’t usually get to do this so they’re kind of loving the media attention maybe,” Agent W wrote.

Agent G.A. said in a subsequent deposition interview that he wanted to be removed from Operation At Large because of the controversial operation outside Newsom’s press conference, as well as internal pressure to carry out what he worried were possible violations of a temporary restraining order.

“It seemed to be pushing into public spaces, you know, more and more frequently,” Agent G.A. told a lawyer during the deposition, which was also included in the ACLU’s court filings. “It seemed to be escalating to less and less targeted.”

Agent G.A. and Agent W’s conversation in the exhibit spans from Aug. 11, 2025, to Aug. 15, 2025. At the time, a federal district court had issued a temporary restraining order that stopped federal agencies from conducting indiscriminate immigration stops. The Supreme Court later paused that ruling on Sept. 8, 2025.

The federal agents questioned among themselves whether they could be held liable for continuing the indiscriminate stops, despite the restraining order. Agent G.A. said they were no longer assigned to Home Depot raids after complaining to management that the raids could violate the court order.

Agent W said they were “pretty sure” the raids violated the order, and said they had signed up for professional liability insurance.

“Still they shouldn’t ask us to do anything that violates a court order,” Agent G.A. said.

“I think they only know one way to operate,” Agent W replied. “See bodies, chase bodies.”

entries.title: Maine Makes Its Legal Case for Kneecapping Super PACs
entries.summary: But in federal court today, free speech advocates defended the right of political donors to make unlimited contributions to certain political groups.
entries.content:
In a federal appeals court in Boston on Wednesday, free speech advocates sparred with the state of Maine and an allied nonprofit organization that want to cap unlimited contributions to super PACs and other big-money political groups.

The state of Maine and Equal Citizens, a nonprofit group founded by Harvard law professor and erstwhile presidential candidate Larry Lessig, are fighting to restore a Maine law capping individual contributions to certain big-spending political groups, such as super PACs, at $5,000.

They’re hoping to take their case all the way to the Supreme Court.

But they faced stiff resistance Wednesday from opponents who argue that spending by outside political groups — groups that raise and spend money to influence elections but are not allowed to coordinate directly with candidates — is a protected form of political speech.

Two super PACs, Dinner Table Action and For Our Future, sued Maine state election officials — successfully — to stop the law, which Maine voters overwhelmingly approved in 2024, from going into effect.

“The American people have a First Amendment right to assemble and to associate, to engage in political speech, and particularly election-related speech, free of infringement from many laws,” Charles "Chip" Miller, a senior attorney at the Institute for Free Speech, which is representing the super PACs, said Wednesday. “That is what we're here talking about today. That's what independent expenditures are. It's the association of individuals to get together to speak.”

But Americans across the political spectrum overwhelmingly believe there is too much money in U.S. politics, according to recent polling by Politico, Pew Research Center and others.

The 2026 midterm election is expected to be the most expensive non-presidential cycle on record, with well-funded super PACs — including the president’s MAGA Inc. and those controlled by cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence and sports-betting industries — poised to play a major role in shaping the election landscape.

Maine is one of several states that’s attempted to limit the amount of money flowing into their elections, which has exploded since 2010, when the Supreme Court greenlit unlimited spending by outside groups in its Citizens United v. FEC decision.

“This case presents a single question: When the people of Maine decided, by the largest vote in the state's 206-year history, that unlimited super PAC contributions were corrupting their elections, did the First Amendment leave them powerless? It did not,” Neal Katyal, a partner at Milbank LLP, who successfully argued against President Donald Trump’s tariffs at the Supreme Court earlier this year, said during oral arguments Wednesday.

Lessig previously told the Maine Morning Star he had expected a legal challenge, and Equal Citizens joined the case to defend the contribution limits.

Lessig’s stated goal is to get the case to the Supreme Court, which he argues hasn’t grappled directly with the constitutionality of unlimited political contributions.

A few months after the Citizens United decision, a federal appeals court in D.C. applied the Supreme Court ruling to another case called SpeechNow.org v. FEC. The court ruled then that contribution limits, not just spending limits, were lawful, as did other appeals courts — and this is the precedent Maine and Equal Citizens are targeting.

“The strategy is to get this case to the Supreme Court with the First Circuit coming into contradiction with the precedents of other Circuits including the Second, Fifth, Seventh, Ninth, Tenth — and, most importantly, the DC Circuit,” Maia Cook, Equal Citizens’ executive director, wrote in a statement to NOTUS.

In a written statement to NOTUS ahead of oral argument, Miller said the Maine ballot measure “strikes at the heart of the First Amendment by severely limiting political speech.”

“There is no legitimate government interest in limiting contributions to groups that make only independent expenditures,” Miller wrote.

The odds that the case makes it to the Supreme Court would rise if the federal appeals court sides with Maine and Equal Citizens, which would create a tantalizing “circuit split” for the court.

Last July, a U.S. magistrate judge stopped Maine from enforcing the law, which she called “unconstitutional on its face.”

The federal appeals court is expected to rule in November or December, although there’s no official timeline for releasing the decision.

Even if the case gets to the Supreme Court, however, Maine faces an uphill battle.

Conservative justices have sympathized with arguments that super PACs erode the power of political parties, in part fueling their decision last month to strike down coordination limits between political party committees and candidates.

But that doesn’t mean justices are willing to limit super PACs’ ability to spend as much money as they want to advocate for or against political candidates.

“[D]onors can and do send their funds to Super PACs and other outside groups that have a First Amendment right to receive and spend unlimited money to support their independent political speech,” conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the opinion last month.

entries.title: Schumer Says He and Troy Jackson Are 'Working Together'
entries.summary: The Maine Senate candidate has said in past interviews that he would not support Schumer as leader next year.
entries.content:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said he met with Democratic Maine Senate hopeful Troy Jackson Wednesday morning.

“We had a great meeting this morning,” Schumer told reporters. “We're working together to win the seat, beat Susan Collins and take back the Senate.”

It’s the first time the New York Democrat has publicly commented on the race since calling for Graham Platner to drop out of the race after sexual assault allegations.

None of Jackson’s potential Senate colleagues have endorsed him since the Maine Democratic Party selected him as the new nominee last Saturday, according to his endorsements page. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) had endorsed Jackson during his earlier gubernatorial run this year. That support has not carried over to Jackson’s Senate campaign: Sanders campaigned heavily for Platner before the allegations broke.

Jackson, like several Senate candidates this cycle, has said he would not support Schumer as leader next year.

“The Democratic Party needs to have a different approach — getting people back in the party, getting working-class, everyday people back in the party — and I don’t believe it’s going to happen with Senator Schumer,” Jackson said in an interview with The New York Times earlier this month.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee backed Jackson’s nomination after it was made official.

“Troy Jackson is a fifth-generation logger with a demonstrated ability to win,” Schumer and Chair Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York) said in a statement that day. “A champion for affordable health care and working people, Jackson has harnessed the grassroots energy in Maine and is well-positioned to defeat Susan Collins, who is more vulnerable than she has ever been.”

Jackson has also earned the endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris, who won Maine by nearly 7 percentage points during her presidential run in 2024.

entries.title: Democrats Can’t Recast Ballots Ahead of Wisconsin Gubernatorial Primary, Judge Rules
entries.summary: The state party filed a lawsuit earlier this month after multiple candidates dropped out of the governor’s race and one candidate re-entered.
entries.content:
Wisconsin voters returned more than 117,000 absentee ballots before one of the front-runners in the governor’s race dropped out and another contender jumped back in — but a judge ruled Wednesday that those voters are not allowed to request new ones.

The ruling shut down a lawsuit filed by the state’s Democratic Party against the Wisconsin Elections Commission to allow the absentee voters to submit new ballots because of the race’s changing nature.

“The unambiguous language of the statute does not allow a voter to spoil an absentee ballot after it is returned,” Dane County Circuit Judge David Conway wrote in his ruling, referencing the guidance the state elections commission rolled out earlier this month on voters’ ability to receive new ballots.

Wisconsin Democratic Party Chair Devin Remiker denounced Conway’s decision and tied the commission’s decision to larger efforts to “suppress” mail-in voting.

“The decision to change the rules around voting that were a long-standing practice before Republicans' attempts to suppress absentee voting was wrong, and we disagree with the ruling today,” Remiker wrote in a statement — adding that the state party intends to “examine all of [their] options moving forward.”

“Their primary is already chaotic enough,” Wisconsin Republican Party Chairman Brian Schimming told The Associated Press earlier this month about the lawsuit. “Election laws should not be changed to rescue one party from the consequences of its own actions.”

Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, who was seen as a front-runner in the governor’s race, dropped out on July 17 after reporting “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in her campaign finance filings. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley jumped back into the race on July 18 — after he’d dropped out on July 8 and endorsed Rodriguez — with support from retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.

Missy Hughes, former Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation CEO, suspended her campaign earlier this month — triggering a decision by the state elections commission to block the ability to revote if a candidate drops out.

The commission voted 4-2 on July 9 to issue the guidance limiting voters’ ability to “spoil” their ballots and excluded circumstances like someone deciding to vote for another candidate.

In their suit, Democrats urged the court to issue a temporary restraining order against the policy.

Rodriguez’s and Hughes’ names remain on ballots, and the primary election is Aug. 11.

Five Democratic candidates — Crowley, former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, former Milwaukee mayoral chief of staff Joel Brennan, state Rep. Francesca Hong and state Sen. Kelda Roys — are still in the running for the Democratic nomination.

entries.title: Redacted Fauci Diary Entries Depict Him Personally Helping Katie Miller
entries.summary: Katie Miller, who has since called for infectious disease doctor Anthony Fauci to be jailed, has said Fauci’s diary entries are self-aggrandizing.
entries.content:
Former White House official and conservative influencer Katie Miller heralded the release of Anthony Fauci’s diaries as a bombshell discovery that outed him as a calculating attention-seeker.

“The most disturbing part of Fauci’s diary — is what he decided to memorialize versus what he kept out of his diary,” she wrote in a post on X on Monday. “It’s almost like he knew this diary would one day become public. He wanted to cast himself as the hero, as famous, as the savior.”

Katie Miller, who is married to Trump adviser and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, has called for Fauci to be jailed. She derided Fauci’s appearance in front of the Senate Wednesday, questioning why he repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment. And she’s said he caused “decades of harm” to children as a leader of the federal government’s COVID-19 response.

Since-redacted excerpts from Fauci’s diary indicate his relationship with Katie Miller was not always this way.

In entries dated to 2020, Fauci’s diary suggests he had a close relationship with Katie Miller, who was Vice President Mike Pence’s communications director at the time and heavily involved in the White House’s COVID-19 response.

Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul, a longtime critic of Fauci’s, published more than 1,000 pages of the infectious disease doctor’s diary Saturday. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told Fox News that he handed the entries over to Senate Republicans after finding them on government servers.

Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergies and Infectious Diseases who served as the face of the Trump administration’s COVID-19 response, writes about providing medical advice to Katie and Stephen Miller. He writes that he counseled the family after Katie Miller tested positive for COVID-19 while pregnant in 2020, when Stephen Miller tested positive and when their newborn child experienced a medical episode later that year.

“I am calling katie frequently to check on her couple time per day. She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone,” Fauci wrote in an entry dated May 9, 2020.

In another entry, Fauci writes that he called the doctors of Miller’s child directly to discuss the infant’s medical care.

Some of the entries detailing Fauci’s interactions with Miller were made public in the initial document dump, but were later redacted.

A NOTUS analysis comparing the originally posted document and the document available Wednesday afternoon show many of the redactions included sections of the diary recounting Fauci’s interactions with the Millers. The original document mentioned Katie Miller 56 times, while the redacted document mentioned her 37 times.

Katie Miller requested that NOTUS not disclose the details of her child’s medical history and said Paul’s office published them without her knowledge or permission. Paul’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

She said that while she and Fauci were in regular contact during the initial COVID-19 response and would occasionally discuss nonwork matters, her opinion of him at the time was that he was “incredibly self-centered and sought to promote himself above the good of the people.”

“He was not my doctor. He was not my friend. He was a work colleague who called me for work purposes, and in the course of a phone call, you would discuss other things,” Miller told NOTUS.

She said she purposely gave Fauci the impression that she was friendly with him so that he “did not leak against me or my husband.”

“I understood who he was, and I understood how to manage somebody like him,” she said. She pointed to a passage in Fauci’s diaries where he describes agreeing with Stephen Miller on the need for border restrictions to prevent the spread of COVID-19.

“How did Stephen Miller manage to get Dr. Fauci there?” she asked rhetorically. “It’s understanding how to communicate with somebody who wants to put themselves above others.”

In recent years, Katie Miller served as the media representative for Kennedy during the presidential transition and as an aide to Elon Musk’s DOGE initiative. Since leaving the administration, she has hosted Kennedy on her podcast. She’s also talked about not vaccinating her youngest child.

Fauci’s diary entries depict Katie Miller as a frequent ally while the Coronavirus Task Force was active and someone he relied on to help sort out issues with Trump and Pence.

“katie Miller is great (tough, smart,but great),” Fauci wrote on March 25, 2020.

Fauci did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Katie Miller, in turn, went to him when her husband tested positive for COVID-19 in the fall of 2020, Fauci wrote.

After Stephen Miller tested positive, Fauci writes, he spoke to Katie multiple times as she was traveling to her parents’ home in Texas. “Spoke to her at Houston airport and after she landed,” he wrote in an entry dated October 6, 2020.

“Am on phone frequently with katie and Stephen,” Fauci wrote on December 31, 2020.

Fauci’s depiction of their relationship in 2020 stands in sharp contrast to the opinions Miller has expressed about Fauci in recent years.

“From the first day of the COVID task force, Dr. Fauci cared more about virtue signaling than science,” Katie Miller wrote in a 2025 post on X.

For some, including former members of the Trump administration, Fauci has come to symbolize government overreach and hubris in the wake of the pandemic. He became the subject of conspiracy theories claiming the federal government covered up the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic and widespread negative reactions to the vaccine. Neither theory has been supported by evidence.

Nevertheless, in anticipation of attempts to prosecute the former health official, former President Joe Biden issued a preemptive pardon for any offenses Fauci may have committed “related to his service as Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, as a member of the White House Coronavirus Task Force or the White House” before leaving office.

Paul, an outspoken critic of Fauci’s, compelled him to appear before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Government Affairs Wednesday.

During the hearing, Fauci, now 85, said in his opening statement that Paul had an “unhinged obsession” with putting him behind bars.

“Given Senator Paul’s obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution, his repeated slanderous comments about me, and recently his publicly releasing my unredacted personal diary aimed at embarrassing and intimidating me, the only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this Committee is to get me to say something that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars,’” Fauci said.

Miller herself has also called for Fauci’s prosecution. When former Director of National Security Tulsi Gabbard released documents last month she claimed showed that Fauci directed funds toward “dangerous” biological research in China, Miller wrote on X, “When asked this question in the Situation Room during the COVID Task Force meetings six years ago, Dr. Fauci said no. Dr. Fauci used the government's medical establishment to push an agenda that protected and promoted himself at the expense of the American people. His autopen pardon should be trashed, and he should be in jail.”

That’s a stark departure from the relationship Fauci wrote about in his diary.

“katie Miller and I laugh at each other in the Sit Room,” he wrote on May 6, 2020.

entries.title: More Migrant Kids Are Getting Removal Orders. Some Could Lose Their Attorneys Too.
entries.summary: A contract for nonprofits representing thousands of children is set to expire Friday.
entries.content:
Nonprofits representing more than 24,000 unaccompanied migrant kids said they’re at risk of shuttering their programs once a federal government contract ends Friday.

The Acacia Center for Justice, which distributes the reimbursements to nearly 100 other legal providers, is nearing the end of its contract. Meanwhile, nonprofits have sued to get the Department of Health and Human Services to pay invoices dating back to December totaling roughly $65 million, the groups said during a press conference Wednesday.

The Trump administration sought to terminate the contract for the minors’ legal representation in March 2025, and the next month a federal judge ordered it to continue funding the work. A hearing to enforce that court order is scheduled for Aug. 6.

Between the end of the contract and millions in unpaid services, some groups are preparing to wind down their services and close the programs representing unaccompanied minors, including some who remain in custody of HSS’ Office of Refugee Resettlement, or ORR.

“The government's actions have been devastating,” said Melissa Lopez, executive director of Estrella del Paso, which provides legal representation to 243 children clients in west Texas and southern New Mexico. “I had to have a conversation with our team yesterday to let them know that based on the way things are happening, our program will close on Friday. We have tried everything we can to avoid that.”

A lack of legal representation would lead to children facing immigration court proceedings alone as deportation orders balloon. Immigration judges issued removal orders for more than 18,000 kids in June, a 73% increase from January, according to data from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

Children represented by The Door in New York City have 28 asylum interviews in the coming weeks, said Meena Shah, managing director of the organization’s legal services center.

“To think about the pressure that is on these young people,” Shah said. “None of us on this call want to abandon our clients.”

In court filings, attorneys for HHS argue the department hasn't paid the invoices because Acacia has not provided specific information about the children’s cases needed to verify that the services are covered under the contract.

The government does not dissuade children from seeking legal relief, an ORR spokesperson said in an email.

“ORR offered Acacia the opportunity to receive a second bridge based on requirements that include they provide the data on who they represent and that they bill us when they submit applications for immigration relief,” the spokesperson said. “Acacia refused to accept this bridge.”

The government had never requested that information before, and turning it over would violate the children’s privacy, the nonprofits have said. Some of the nonprofits — Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, Ayuda, and Kids in Need of Defense — said in June that HHS and Homeland Security Investigations officers tried to access financial records relating to the minor clients at their Washington, D.C.-area offices.

“They continue to insist that the only way that they will pay for the work already completed for the representation of children is if we betray our legal ethics and the confidences of children who we are representing,” Shaina Aber, executive director at Acacia, said during a press conference last week. “Obviously, that's not tenable.”

Since January 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has arrested thousands of unaccompanied minors and their sponsors, who are usually family members, based on leads from ORR, Reuters reported.

In June, ORR had 1,796 children in its custody, who on average are spending 194 days in the government’s care, according to the department’s most recent data. Children spent longer in ORR custody in the last fiscal year than during the first Trump administration.

HHS did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment about how the unaccompanied minors would receive legal services once the Acacia contract ends.

But the Trump administration has asked the Texas Attorney General’s office and Texas Indigent Defense Commission for help representing the kids, The Texas Tribune reported. The Department of Defense has also prepared to task military lawyers for the job, Bloomberg reported.

entries.title: Chris Murphy Demands Answers From Education Department Over Disputed Civics Competition
entries.summary: The contest’s results left the family of Aangad Singh “reeling,” Murphy wrote to Secretary Linda McMahon, calling for a detailed explanation of the scoring.
entries.content:
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy demanded “transparency” from the Department of Education Wednesday regarding the disputed results of a national civics contest for high school students.

“This competition was supposed to be a celebration of this nation’s founding, uplifting principles of equality and justice,” Murphy wrote in the letter addressed to Education Secretary Linda McMahon, exclusively obtained by NOTUS. “Instead, the Presidential 1776 Award’s opaque rules and scoring have cast serious doubts about basic standards of fairness and left a family reeling.”

The Connecticut senator wrote on behalf of Aangad Singh, the 15-year-old Connecticut boy who competed, and his family, who are seeking to understand why Singh did not advance to the finals. The controversy, first reported by NOTUS, has drawn national scrutiny over whether the results were rigged or biased against a boy of Indian descent in favor of three finalists who fit President Donald Trump’s education agenda.

One was home-schooled, another attended a private, Catholic school, and the third, who went to public school, told CNN that she supported Trump and believed the most important thing was “everyone walking away from the competition knowing this is the greatest country of the world.”

“The students who won the competition were undeniably impressive,” Murphy wrote. “However, it is easy to understand why groups like the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus have suggested the competition was biased since the Trump Administration has made clear it believes anyone who is not a white male is inferior. Through hateful rhetoric, sweeping executive orders, and devastating funding cuts, Trump has turned discrimination into a governing agenda.”

Murphy, who sits on two Senate committees that oversee the Department of Education, requested “a full review of the results,” including detailed explanations for disputed answers and any scoring documents. He set a Sept. 1 deadline for the department to respond.

“We are very grateful to Senator Murphy and his team for raising these questions, and we hope this will help us finally receive clear answers,” Bhalindar Singh, Aangad’s father, said.

The Department of Education did not respond to a request for comment.

CBS broadcast the Presidential 1776 Award competition on June 30, and immediately, Singh and his family questioned the results.

According to their analysis, two of Aangad’s answers were incorrectly scored as wrong, and if either had been scored correctly, he would have advanced to the final three. The finalists received a share of $250,000 in scholarships and a trip to the Oval Office to meet the president.

The first disputed answer was about the finer points of Article 3 of the U.S. Constitution. The second was about which amendment ended slavery. To the latter question, Singh said “13th,” according to auto-generated subtitles, which was correct. But on the broadcast, it was marked as wrong.

“His answer to question two is undeniably correct,” Murphy wrote. “As has been publicly reported, there is some debate about how to score his answer to question one, but his answer is clearly at least partially correct.”

On July 14, Aangad’s father asked the Education Department to review his son’s scores. A week later, an aide to McMahon wrote back that the “judges exercised independent good faith judgment in selecting finalists and winners.”

“The graphics shown in the broadcast accurately reflected the points awarded by the judges’ interpretation of answers and scoring,” the aide said.

The response did not engage with the substance of their questions, Aangad’s father said, and Murphy echoed the sentiments in his letter.

In an initial statement to NOTUS before the story was published, an Education Department spokesperson said any questions about the integrity of the competition should be directed to the James Madison Memorial Fellowship Foundation, the federal organization that it said independently developed, judged and scored the questions.

As Education secretary, McMahon holds one of the foundation’s two active board seats. None of the five judges responded to multiple requests for comment. The panel scholar, Abbylin Sellers, initially agreed to an interview but then canceled, saying, “I have informed the Department of Ed press team of your request and will let them handle it.”

Roger Jones III, the principal at a Tennessee high school where one of the judges teaches social studies, said in an email that he was not aware of the controversy and referred questions to the foundation.

“While the James Madison Memorial Fellowship Foundation may have provided the judges,” Murphy wrote to McMahon, “it is incumbent upon the Department to clarify the results as the host of this official competition put on by the federal government.”

Murphy’s letter is the latest twist in a relationship that can seem like a storyline straight out of the wrestling organization McMahon once helped run.

In 2012, Murphy and McMahon, a former WWE executive, battled for the Senate seat Murphy now occupies, a race that Murphy won by 15 percentage points. McMahon spent a record $100 million in personal funds on two unsuccessful Senate bids — she also lost in 2010 to Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal.

Five years later, Trump nominated McMahon to lead the Small Business Administration. During her confirmation process, Murphy struck a more conciliatory tone. He voted for her confirmation and said in a statement that, “while Linda and I haven’t always seen eye-to-eye, I look forward to working with her to help small businesses in Connecticut."

In 2025, when Trump returned to office, they went back to battling.

During McMahon’s confirmation hearing to lead the Education Department, Murphy, who sits on the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, pressed her about how an executive order restricting federal funding for DEI programs would impact schools.

“It is good to see you again outside of the state of Connecticut, where we run into each other,” she replied.

This time, he voted against her nomination. The committee advanced her on a 12-11, party-line vote, and she was ultimately confirmed.

entries.title: Major D.C. Law Firm Details Theft From Political Committee
entries.summary: The Arnold & Porter PAC told federal regulators a thief stole paper checks from mailboxes in Washington’s upscale Cleveland Park neighborhood.
entries.content:
A thief stole, then altered, multiple political contribution checks sent through the mail by the political action committee of a major Washington-based law firm, according to a new letter to federal regulators NOTUS reviewed.

The unidentified thief stole two of the checks from a batch of political donation payments the Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer LLP’s PAC mailed in D.C.’s upscale Cleveland Park neighborhood on Nov. 24, 2025.

Arnold & Porter subsequently increased its security protocols, enrolling in Truist bank’s fraud inspector program, which generates an email to the committee “every time a payment is debited from its bank account,” allowing the PAC to dispute any unauthorized payments.

Arnold & Porter’s Wednesday letter to the Federal Election Commission provides these and other new details about the theft, which NOTUS first revealed in June. And it arrives amid a rash of thefts involving federal political committees, including revelations this week involving the cash-strapped Democratic National Committee and the Senate campaign of Michigan Republican Mike Rogers.

The law firm’s PAC described the unknown party that carried out the theft as a “criminal actor” who intercepted and washed the checks — changing the payee and dollar amount.

Arnold & Porter’s treasurer, Nicholas L. Townsend, told the FEC that the thief altered one check intended for the campaign committee of Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York). After stealing the check, the thief changed the written value — $1,000 — to $40,000 and made it out to "Gleora Agoj" with "Advisory Asistant fee" written on the memo line.

The name on the check does not appear to be affiliated with Arnold & Porter. The Meeks campaign never received the funds, according to the memo.

Another check addressed to the American Mosaic PAC, a committee focused on increasing diversity in Congress, was altered from $2,500 to $20,953.

The Arnold & Porter PAC discovered “that at least one check, and possibly more, had not been received by the intended recipients” and put “stop-payment requests” on the disbursements to Meeks’ campaign and the American Mosaic PAC.

The law firm, which is headquartered in D.C., called Truist on May 1 after it noticed multiple unauthorized payments and the “two suspicious check deposits pending” while compiling its monthly financial report to the FEC.

The bank assured Arnold & Porter that the committee’s account would not be charged, but the $40,000 was still taken from the PAC’s funds. The $20,000 check was never honored by the bank because of the stop-payment order, Townsend told the FEC.

The Arnold & Porter committee ultimately recouped the $40,000 in stolen funds from the fraudulent check and an additional $2,700 unauthorized payments through the bank.
ArnoldPorter (1250x887, AR: 1.41)Following the theft, the committee told the FEC it had taken several steps, including enrollment in its bank’s fraud detection program, to address any security or information gaps in its payment processes.

“The Committee also submitted an incident report to the U.S. Postal Service stating that someone was stealing mail in the neighborhood,” Townsend wrote.

Arnold & Porter did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the memo.

Check fraud is generally on the rise across the nation, with suspicious activity reports, or documents filed by financial institutions to report suspected violations of the law, nearly doubling from 2021 to 2023, according to the FBI.

entries.title: Boozman Plans Senate Farm Bill Markup Without Clear Bipartisan Deal
entries.summary: The Agriculture Committee chair says he is working “to see if we can get a path forward.”
entries.content:
The chair of the Senate Agriculture Committee said Wednesday that the panel will take up the farm bill late next week, despite what has been a partisan deadlock on the measure.

Sen. John Boozman (R-Arkansas) told reporters he is working closely with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota), the committee’s ranking member, “to see if we can get a path forward” and that details are still being worked out.

“We've got a good bill. I think lots of our members and both sides want to support it,” Boozman said.

But Klobuchar, in a statement from her office, said there is still plenty of ground to cover.

"We're continuing to have productive negotiations, but there is a lot of work left to do. Senate Ag Democrats have been clear that a Farm Bill must meet the needs of both farmers and families across America,” Klobuchar said in a statement.

Boozman did not go into details of the negotiations, but any deal is likely to include some compromise on when states must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, a change Republicans put in a previous law.

Democrats have asked for a two-year delay in the cost shift for states with error rates above 6%, with one calling the request a “deal-maker and a deal-breaker.” Republicans have preferred to leave the changes made to SNAP from the “one big, beautiful bill” last year.

Boozman also said he is still unsure whether Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) will be present for the committee's markup. McConnell has been recovering from an illness and unable to participate, leaving the committee tied with 11 Republican and Democratic members each.

“We're going to go forward regardless. I've always said for a farm to be successful it needs to be bipartisan,” Boozman said. “So that’s what we’re working on getting done.”

Even if Republicans can advance the farm bill from the committee without Democratic support, it does not appear to have enough support to overcome the 60-vote threshold needed to advance on the Senate floor, since Democrats say they would not support the bill without a SNAP cost-shift delay.

A markup, which would be the first time the committee has voted on a farm bill since 2018, is tied to a hard deadline.The current extension of the 2018 farm bill runs through Sept. 30. The House passed its version of the farm bill on April 30.

entries.title: Trump Announces $22 Billion Renovation for ‘Impossible’ Dulles Airport
entries.summary: “Basic disasters” is how the president described two of the terminals that would be replaced.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump shared plans on Wednesday for a massive, $22 billion construction and renovation project at Washington Dulles International Airport.

The president, who’s pushing forward on projects to revamp iconic sites around Washington, D.C., showcased a scale model and pictures of the proposed new hub that would do away with the infamous “people movers,” add thousands of parking stalls and replace entire terminals.

“We are announcing plans to add more than 5 million square feet of new or renovated space,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “We'll replace the current C and D concourses, which are basic disasters, all the while preserving the iconic original terminal.”

The architect Eero Saarinen completed the original terminal in 1962, the same year the airport, about 25 miles west of Washington, opened. The terminal’s iconic mid-century modern architecture features concrete columns and a concave cable roof.

Trump described Saarinen as “one of the great architects of the world,” but said the original terminal was both an “asset and a liability” because “nobody wanted to build anything near it.”

The airport could also get a new 32,000-space parking garage, which Trump said will be the largest in the world. The current largest parking complex is in Edmonton, Canada, with parking for about 20,000 vehicles.

United Airlines, which has a major hub at Dulles, described the timeline for the project as being completed “over the next decade.” Construction could start in the spring.

The project proposes do away with the fleet of people movers, which function like buses, transporting flyers between terminals.

“It's an impossible airport. You get off a bus, you go into a train, you get from a train, you get onto another bus,” Trump said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a “horseshoe train system” would replace the people movers and provide travelers with “easy access to all of your gates.”

The administration reviewed designs from more than 30 architects, and the president described the project as a “bipartisan” effort.

“Whether you're a Republican or Democrat, you don't want to go and be subjected to this airport because this airport, it's a terrible place to be,” Trump said.

United Airlines will help pay for the project, which is set to include the largest United Polaris lounge in the world, according to Trump.

“This is not requiring federal dollars,” Jack Potter, president and CEO of the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, told reporters. “This is going to be airport-generated dollars, airline contributions — which is phenomenal.”

Trump said doing the airport construction “all at one time” would allow the project to be completed in a few years, far less than the original 60-year estimate if it was broken up into stages.

“It's time to ensure that the United States has the greatest airports anywhere in the world, and we're starting right here with the capital city,” Trump said.
